waypoints.name: US-2 roadside pullout at WSDOT maintenance yard
waypoints.note: Unmarked shoulder pullout on US-2 at the WSDOT maintenance yard turnoff (room for several cars); no permit required, no official trailhead signage.
waypoints.directions: Park at the unmarked shoulder pullout on US-2 by the WSDOT maintenance and tunnel-entrance yard, roughly 6 to 7 miles east of Stevens Pass. There is room for two or three cars and no permit is needed, but check for posted no-parking signs. Nothing here is signed — there is no trailhead, no trail number and no maintained tread anywhere on this route.

waypoints.name: Nason Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the highway then ford Nason Creek just past the FR 687/bridge area on the climbers' path; can run high and cold during spring snowmelt.
waypoints.directions: Walk back west along the highway shoulder and cross to the north side just past the Nason Creek bridge. Pick up the climbers' path and get across the creek; it runs high and cold during spring snowmelt.

waypoints.name: BNSF railroad grade crossing
waypoints.note: Route briefly follows the old railroad/powerline grade paralleling the creek and crosses the active BNSF Stevens Pass line (Empire Builder route) — look both ways, trains run frequently.
waypoints.directions: On the far side the route joins the old railroad and powerline grade running beside the creek, which means crossing the active BNSF Stevens Pass main line. Trains use this corridor frequently — look both ways and do not linger on the tracks.

waypoints.name: Leave grade, begin timbered ascent
waypoints.note: About 1 mile from the highway the route leaves the railroad/powerline grade and scrambles up a steep timbered bank — this is the start of the unmarked climb to the northeast ridge.
waypoints.directions: Follow the grade (Forest Road 687) roughly east-southeast alongside Nason Creek for about a mile, ducking under a set of powerlines and skirting standing runoff ponds in the first ten to fifteen minutes. At around 2,700 ft leave the grade and scramble up the creek-cut bank into the timber. Nothing marks the spot, so pick your line off the map rather than looking for a path.

waypoints.name: Minor cliff bands in the timber
waypoints.note: Short rock cliff bands force route-finding through the trees around 3,400 ft; stay alert for the path of least resistance to avoid getting cliffed out.
waypoints.directions: Climb steep, wooded slopes on a compass bearing, over downed logs and loose duff, with old blue and yellow forestry blazes on some trees. Around 3,400 ft short rock bands break the slope — work around them at the path of least resistance rather than pressing straight up, since the terrain here is broken enough to cliff you out.

waypoints.name: Gain the northeast shoulder/ridge
waypoints.note: Steep timber eases onto the mountain's northeast ridge here (reported 4,600-4,800 ft); turn and follow the ridge crest through heather and talus toward the summit.
waypoints.directions: The timber stays steep above the rock bands until the angle eases onto the crest somewhere between 4,600 and 4,800 ft. Snow cover usually starts near 3,700 ft and can be firm or icy under the tree canopy even when it is soft in the open, so this is where most parties put on microspikes or snowshoes.

waypoints.name: Arrowhead Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit (6,030 ft) with views of Glacier Peak, the Chiwaukum Mountains, and Jim Hill Mountain; no register commonly reported.
waypoints.directions: From the shoulder, turn and follow the crest southeast through open glades, heather and talus to the summit rocks. The angle eases here and the going is the easiest of the day, but the route stays unmarked to the top and the clearcut edges along this stretch make it easy to drift off the crest.

waypoints.name: Holden Village / Railroad Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Access via Lady of the Lake ferry to Lucerne then the Holden Village shuttle bus; standard-route parties stage here.
waypoints.directions: There is no road in. Take the Lake Chelan ferry from Chelan or Field's Point to Lucerne, then the village shuttle up from the landing. Plan the whole trip around the boat and bus timetable in both directions — parties who miss the connection out spend an extra night at the village.

waypoints.name: Railroad Creek Trail / Holden Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the valley-bottom trail here and climb toward Holden Lake on dry, open-pine switchbacks.
waypoints.directions: Walk the gravel road and Railroad Creek Trail (FST 1256) west out of the village for about a mile. The Holden Lake Trail leaves it on the right and is signed.

waypoints.name: Holden Lake
waypoints.note: Common base camp in a glacial basin directly below the Mary Green Glacier; water is scarce on the approach so fill up here.
waypoints.directions: Steady climbing for several miles through forest and brush, with a few small side creeks that run reliably. Black flies are thick through the lower part of this stretch. The trail ends in the cirque directly under Bonanza's east face.

waypoints.name: Holden Pass high camp
waypoints.note: Alternate, higher camp that most summit parties use to shorten summit day; some brushy bushwhacking to reach it.
waypoints.directions: From the lake outlet the tread fades out. Skirt the north shore through slide alder and talus — genuine bushwhacking and route-finding, worse early season when the water is high — then climb a hillside traverse northwest to the pass.

waypoints.name: Mary Green Glacier, north edge
waypoints.note: Rising traverse to a snowfield below slabs, then a scramble onto the glacier's north edge — rope up for the crossing here.
waypoints.directions: Rising traverse west from the pass along the ridge and slope to a snowfield beneath rock slabs at roughly 7,000 to 7,300 ft. Scramble the class 3 slabs above it, starting high and to the right to keep clear of a waterfall. The gullies here sit below a retreating glacier margin and are loose, so stay out of the fall line and out from under any party above you.

waypoints.name: Moat crossing, glacier's upper corner
waypoints.note: Cross the moat via a snow bridge onto rock; bridges can collapse by late season, sometimes forcing a detour right onto rock.
waypoints.directions: Bear west along the glacier's north (climber's right) edge, then traverse southwest under the base of Bonanza's northeast ridge to the glacier's upper corner. Finish up the steep snow finger to its high point and look for the exit onto rock; an overhanging snow lip can be as much of an obstacle as the moat itself. The crossing gets harder as the season goes on and can turn into a maze of crevasses rather than a single step across.

waypoints.name: Bonanza Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit reached after the moat and a short Class 3-4 finish; descent reverses the route with about four rappels off fixed stations.
waypoints.directions: Off the snow, climb class 3-4 rock just right of a gully for several rope-lengths, then traverse left into a second gully and scramble to a notch on the northeast ridge just north of the top. From the notch follow the crest past a run of large blocks to the summit horn. The rock along here is loose and this is where the route's rockfall problem lives — anything knocked off funnels straight down the gullies onto whoever is below.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road (FR-15), ~23 mi from Marblemount; self-issue wilderness permit required for overnight camping beyond here.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), roughly 23 miles from Marblemount and about 3,600 feet in elevation. Any overnight camping beyond the trailhead requires a self-issue wilderness permit.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass and splits; leave the Pacific Crest/Stehekin trail here and climb north on the Sahale Arm climbers' path toward Sahale Glacier Camp.
waypoints.directions: Well-graded switchbacks through old-growth forest, then a traverse across subalpine meadows to the pass — roughly 3.7 miles and 1,700 ft of gain, and the easiest ground on the whole route.

waypoints.name: Sahale Glacier Camp
waypoints.note: Established high-camp platforms on the glacier moraine; NPS permit and bear canister required, no campfires, and it's fully exposed to wind and afternoon thunderstorms.
waypoints.directions: Turn north and climber's-right onto the Sahale Arm trail and climb steadily through heather meadow, then over steepening rock and scree benches to the toe of the Sahale Glacier. The upper switchbacks and the final scramble into camp are the steepest walking of the approach. The Arm is dry above the meadows, so this is a leg to carry water up rather than expect to find it.

waypoints.name: Sahale-Buckner notch
waypoints.note: Steep, snow-filled cleft on Sahale's south ridge that must be down-climbed frontpointing to drop into Horseshoe Basin; firm snow makes this exposed and fall-prone in early season.
waypoints.directions: Leave camp heading south onto Sahale's south ridge and descend it on snow and easy class 1-2 rock, working either side of the crest as it steepens. A short class 3 face is downclimbed to reach the notch. The same step has to be reclimbed on the way back, so note the line you take down it.

waypoints.name: Horseshoe Basin traverse (Davenport Mine)
waypoints.note: Broad snow bench traverse of roughly 2 miles across the basin passing the ruins of the historic Davenport silver mine; stay on the mid-elevation ledge system to avoid cliffing out.
waypoints.directions: Downclimb the snow-filled cleft below the notch — parties commonly stay in the moat at its edge until forced onto the snow finger, then front-point down to the bench beneath. From the bench traverse across the basin, holding 6,600 to 6,800 ft beneath Ripsaw Ridge for the first mile, then angling up toward the mine ruins. Rockfall crosses this traverse and the snow softens quickly after mid-morning, so it wants doing early.

waypoints.name: Cowskull snowfield / summit couloir
waypoints.note: Steep snow chute leading to a distinctive cowskull-shaped snow patch used as the navigation cue for the final approach; watch for wet slide potential in the afternoon.
waypoints.directions: From the mine keep angling up across steepening southwest-face snowfields, trending more easterly as you come in under the cowskull, then head straight up the snow chute below it. The angle on this section is enough that many parties put in a running belay on pickets rather than solo it.

waypoints.name: Buckner Mountain (southwest summit)
waypoints.note: True summit reached via loose scree/rubble and a final Class 2-3 rock scramble along the summit ridge.
waypoints.directions: Step off the top of the cowskull, take the crampons off, and grovel up loose scree and rubble to gain the south ridge near 8,800 ft. About a hundred feet of class 2-3 rock along the crest finishes it. All of this last section is loose, so keep the party tight or well out of each other's fall line.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead (SR-20 milepost 134)
waypoints.note: North Cascades NP wilderness permit required; a 0.6-mile spur trail drops to the Ross Lake shoreline where the multi-day approach to Castle Peak begins.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is a pullout on SR-20 near milepost 134. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required before you start.

waypoints.name: Ross Lake Dock / Boat Put-in
waypoints.note: Put-in for the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (or paddle) that shortcuts many miles of the East Bank Trail toward the Lightning Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: A 0.6-mile spur trail drops from the pullout to the Ross Lake shoreline, losing about a hundred feet. Anyone bringing a private or inflatable boat portages it down this stretch.

waypoints.name: Lightning Creek Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Boat drop-off where the route leaves Ross Lake and picks up the Lightning Creek Trail heading east into the valley toward Freezeout Creek.
waypoints.directions: The lake crossing runs north to the Lightning Creek landing near the head of Ross Lake. The resort water taxi is the usual way across and books out well in advance; paddling it adds hours at both ends. Either way the return pickup is a fixed time, so plan the summit day around it — there is no quick walk-out from this side.

waypoints.name: Turner Bridge / Nightmare Camp
waypoints.note: Lightning Creek crossing near Nightmare Camp on an aging span; the bridge is unstable and a ford may be required.
waypoints.directions: From the landing follow the Lightning Creek Trail up-valley for roughly seven miles of forest walking. Parties commonly leave the shore before dawn to leave enough daylight for the ground above. The bridge is the Lightning Creek crossing and has been in poor shape; a ford may be the safer option, and that is a call worth making in daylight on the way in rather than by headlamp on the way out.

waypoints.name: Freezeout Creek Cabin
waypoints.note: Maintained backcountry cabin at about 3,600 ft on the abandoned Freezeout Creek Trail, above the steep section where it leaves the Lightning Creek Trail; the last reliably stocked shelter/water stop before the climb proper.
waypoints.directions: Cross Lightning Creek and pick up the old, unmaintained Freezeout Creek Trail. The first stretch above the junction is the trickiest route-finding on the whole approach: steep rock-and-alder slopes that take a rising, diagonal ascent line before you regain proper forest and tread. Flagging has marked it in recent seasons but do not plan on it being there. Back in the trees the tread is in decent shape the rest of the way, and the cabin sits just past a creek crossing.

waypoints.name: Freezeout Creek Ford & Blowdown Zone
waypoints.note: Trail disintegrates into heavy blowdown above the cabin; climbers ford Freezeout Creek and sidehill through alder to regain open talus near 5,000 ft.
waypoints.directions: About a quarter mile above the cabin, cross Freezeout Creek again and pass through an old burn. Tread mostly gives out near 4,200 ft where it turns north and re-crosses the creek, though the bushwhacking through here is not bad. Stay on the west side of the creek roughly 50-100 ft above the water — that band gives the most open going — until about 5,000 ft, where you cross to the south/east side and the ground opens into meadow and talus.

waypoints.name: Southwest Ridge Notch
waypoints.note: Gained via steep red heather and scree slopes; marks the start of the class 2-3 scramble along the SW ridge to the summit.
waypoints.directions: From the open ground above 5,000 ft it is a long, steady climb on steep red heather, talus and scree to the notch — around 2,500 ft of gain with no water on any of it, so fill from the creek before you leave it. Several similar-looking gullies and chutes feed this basin; note the exact one you come up, because taking the wrong one on the way down cliffs you out on bluffs well above the creek.

waypoints.name: Castle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, second-highest peak in the Hozomeen Range, about one mile south of the Canadian border; class 2-3 scrambling on the final pitch.
waypoints.directions: From the notch it is roughly 700 vertical feet along the ridge, mostly Class 2 with short Class 3 steps. The rock is generally good but there is loose talus on it, and the crest is fully exposed with nowhere to shelter — get off it early if storms are building. On this schedule most parties finish the descent in the dark, so carry headlamps regardless of the forecast.

waypoints.name: Beverly Turnpike Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-9737-112 off Beverly Creek Road; cross the stout bridge over Beverly Creek right at the trailhead — Northwest Forest Pass required for parking.
waypoints.directions: Drive the North Fork Teanaway River Road to Beverly Creek Road and follow FR-9737-112 to its end at roughly 3,450-3,600 ft. Wildfire damage has closed this trail system before, so confirm current Forest Service status before committing to the drive in.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek Trail fork
waypoints.note: Beverly Turnpike Trail forks here; leave the Beverly Creek roadbed and turn right (east) up the Bean Creek valley onto Trail #1391.1.
waypoints.directions: Start north on the Beverly Turnpike Trail #1391, a mellow stretch of old roadbed alongside Beverly Creek. At the signed junction bear right and east onto the Bean Creek Trail; the Turnpike Trail carries straight on up the Beverly drainage, which is the wrong valley for this peak.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Bean Creek in a tight, steep valley; can run cold and pushy during June snowmelt, and the trail crosses old avalanche debris just above here.
waypoints.directions: The Bean Creek Trail climbs steadily through forest into a tight, steep-sided valley before dropping to the water. It is an easy rock-hop by mid to late summer, but in May and June snowmelt it runs cold and pushy and is the real decision point of the day; the trail crosses old avalanche debris just above the ford.

waypoints.name: Bean Creek Basin junction
waypoints.note: Trail forks at the edge of subalpine meadows: stay left for Bean Creek Basin's wildflower fields or bear right/east for the Earl Peak saddle approach.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing through forest until it breaks open into the basin — a broad flower meadow with old-growth stands and several informal camping flats. Fill water here. Bean Creek is the last dependable source and there is none above the meadows.

waypoints.name: Earl Pass (southwest ridge gain)
waypoints.note: Saddle on the divide between Bean and Standup Creek drainages; leave the boot path here and gain the southwest ridge toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: At the meadow fork bear right and east rather than continuing left into the upper basin. Tread goes intermittent through the upper meadows before switchbacking up to the broad saddle on the divide, about 2,600 ft of gain in all from the car.

waypoints.name: False summit / loose scree pitch
waypoints.note: Class 1 but exposed to extremely loose, kickable scree on an approximately 70-degree pitch just below the true summit — easy to mistake for the top.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the pass and pick up the intermittent boot track climbing the ridge directly toward the summit. This is the sustained part of the day: roughly 800 vertical feet of unrelenting class 2 on loose scree, sand and broken rock, with the track fading in and out. Go slowly, test what you stand on, and stay out from under anyone above.

waypoints.name: Earl Peak summit
waypoints.note: Talus/heather summit block with views across the Teanaway to Mount Stuart; a short ridge scramble continues north to Bean Peak for those extending the trip.
waypoints.directions: From the false top the remaining ground is short — a few more minutes of the same loose ridge tread and talus over the last rise, with no harder moves than what you have already done.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
waypoints.note: Park off SR-20 near Newhalem at Goodell Creek Campground/road; NPS wilderness permit required for overnight camping in Terror/Crescent Creek Basins.
waypoints.directions: Drive Highway 20 to Newhalem and park at the Goodell Creek Campground and trailhead just off the highway. An NPS wilderness permit is required for overnight camping in the Terror and Crescent Creek Basins, so arrange that before you head in.

waypoints.name: Cairn - Old Roadbed / Terror Basin Fork
waypoints.note: Old logging roadbed ends here; a cairn (replacing an older rock arrow) marks the unmaintained boot path climbing steeply south of Terror Creek toward Terror Basin.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old roadbed and climbers' path up the Goodell Creek valley for about four miles, gaining only around 1,000 ft. Fill water at the junction: this is the last easy, reliable source before the climb steepens.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Log Jam Crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Terror Creek on a log jam; the exact crossing point shifts year to year and can require wading or bushwhacking upstream in high water.
waypoints.directions: Leave the roadbed at the cairn on the unmaintained path cutting uphill and to the right; it reaches Terror Creek within a few hundred yards, before any of the real climbing begins.

waypoints.name: Terror Basin
waypoints.note: Gravelly, wildflower basin with established tent sites and multiple streams; the standard base camp for Southern Pickets objectives, roughly a 7-hour day in.
waypoints.directions: Past the creek the boot path turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 4,000-4,700 ft in well under three horizontal miles through old-growth and brush; expect head-high slide alder and devil's club depending on the season and snow year. It breaks out of timber near 5,000-5,200 ft onto heather benches, slabs and snowfields. The path is boot-beaten but often faint, and there is no dependable water between the creek and the basin.

waypoints.name: The Barrier
waypoints.note: Loose, exposed low-5th-class ridge crossing over a moat divides Terror Basin from Crescent Creek Basin; classic unstable 'Pickets Class 3' terrain, harder late season.
waypoints.directions: From the tent sites, climb up-basin roughly 700 ft to the north-northwest to reach the crest of the divide. The ground is grassy ledges and loose blocks, and it is the one stretch of the approach where a slip has real consequences.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Flat camping area below Mount Terror used as the high camp for Ottohorn, Himmelhorn, and Frenzel Spitz objectives.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft off the far side on mixed snow and talus, steeply at first, then traverse for roughly an hour into the basin under the Ottohorn-Himmelhorn massif to reach the flat ground used for camping.

waypoints.name: Ottohorn-Himmelhorn Col
waypoints.note: Gain the col from Crescent Creek Basin (snow-filled and straightforward early season, loose tricky 5th class if melted out); the descent toward Frenzel Spitz's South Route drops off its north side from here.
waypoints.directions: From the basin camp it is about 1,400 ft and roughly an hour of climbing up to the crest. This Crescent Creek side is the friendly side of the col, loose but moderate 3rd and 4th class; the north side, which drops toward Frenzel Spitz, is sustained loose 5th class, with a steep step that is usually rappelled on the way down and has to be reclimbed on the way back.

waypoints.name: Frenzel Spitz Summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via 5.6 rock on the south side after descending about 500 ft from the col; return the same way, reclimbing to the col.
waypoints.directions: Do not try to follow the crest across. From the col, downclimb roughly 500 ft of broken, frequently snow- or ice-covered ground onto the Frenzel Spitz side to reach the foot of the South Route, then climb its rock at about 5.6 back up to the top. The small net height difference between col and summit hides a full descent and re-ascent, so budget the time for it; the step below the col is commonly rappelled from natural anchors on the way in and reclimbed on the way back.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Old roadbed starts at the Goodell Creek group campground turnout off SR 20 (milepost 119) near Newhalem; NPS wilderness permit required for overnight; no parking pass is needed at this National Park trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 about 60 miles - roughly an hour and a half - east from Burlington and park at the Goodell Creek Campground turnout at milepost 119, just west of Newhalem. The highway is paved all the way to here, and the trailhead sits west of both of SR 20's winter closure gates (Ross Dam at milepost 134, and Newhalem at milepost 120 in harder winters), so driving access to this trailhead does not depend on the seasonal opening of the highway east of the park.

waypoints.name: Roadbed End / Basin Fork
waypoints.note: The 4-mile old roadbed peters out at a stone cairn in a wide clearing; the defined path forks right toward Terror Creek Basin, while a fainter boot path continues straight for the Crescent Creek Basin / Stump Hollow approach used for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and Frenzel Spitz.
waypoints.directions: Follow the old decommissioned logging roadbed upstream along the true left (south) side of Goodell Creek. It is grassy and gravelly, flat and easy walking for roughly 4 to 4.5 miles, gaining only a few hundred feet from the ~600 ft trailhead to about 1,700-1,800 ft. The end of it is not obvious from the tread - watch on the right, in the wide clearing, for the cairn or stone marker climbers call the 'stone arrow', which is what marks the unsigned climbers' path leaving the creek bottom.

waypoints.name: Treeline Breakout
waypoints.note: Boot path breaks out of old-growth forest onto steep heather benches and slab; the steep, brushy tread above the roadbed is easy to lose in fog.
waypoints.directions: Top off water at Goodell Creek before leaving the roadbed: there is none reliable again until treeline. From the cairn, the boot path leaves the creek bottom and switchbacks steeply up into old-growth forest toward Stump Hollow. Expect steep root-and-duff footing with slide alder and devil's club low down; the path stays reasonably distinct with flagging and cairns higher up, but multiple trip reports on this approach describe losing it, and it is especially easy to lose in fog - track it deliberately rather than trusting the tread to hold. Around 5,000-5,600 ft the timber gives way to the heather benches and slab of Stump Hollow, a slabby basin wedged between the Barrier ridge and the Chopping Block.

waypoints.name: Terror-Crescent Divide Saddle
waypoints.note: Rising traverse gains this ~6,200 ft saddle on the ridge dividing Terror Creek and Crescent Creek basins; drop west off the saddle into Crescent Creek Basin from here.
waypoints.directions: From Stump Hollow, make a rising traverse over meadow, slab and - early to mid season - snow to the broad saddle at roughly 6,200 ft on the Barrier, the ridge dividing Terror Creek basin from Crescent Creek basin. Carry an ice axe for this, and crampons early season.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Streams
waypoints.note: Two snowmelt streams run off the slabs above camp; reliable early-to-mid season but reported to thin out by late August in dry years.
waypoints.directions: This leg is the Barrier crossing, the most exposed piece of the approach and one of the route's named hazards. Cross by one of two options: a lower line on a loose, exposed ledge system at the toe of the Terror Glacier, or a higher line over moat terrain and steep choss just below Mt. Degenhardt. Either takes under an hour, but both are loose enough that rockfall onto anyone below is the real hazard - helmets on, and do not stack the party. Drop the far (west) side of the saddle into Crescent Creek Basin, where two snowmelt streams run off the slabs; they are reliable early to mid season but reported to thin out by late August in dry years, so plan your water around that rather than assuming they run.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin Camp
waypoints.note: Established gravel-and-heather camp on slabs used as the base for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn, and Frenzel Spitz; reach it via the stump-hollow traverse rather than the Terror Basin path.
waypoints.directions: A last short step across the gravel and heather slabs from the stream draws to the established basin camp at roughly 5,800 ft below Mt. Terror. This is the standard base for Himmelhorn, Ottohorn and Frenzel Spitz, and it is reached by the Stump Hollow traverse rather than by the Terror Basin path. Camping here is at-large with no designated sites, but an NPS backcountry permit is required for the overnight, and a park-wide moratorium bans new fixed anchors - plan on clean, removable gear for everything above.

waypoints.name: Himmel-Otto Col Gully
waypoints.note: Narrow gully gains the Himmel-Otto col between Himmelhorn and Ottohorn; straightforward snow early season, but by late season expect icy neve, chossy moats, and an overhanging boulder near the top forcing a loose class 3/4 bypass on climber's left.
waypoints.directions: From camp, climb the narrow gully leading to the Himmel-Otto col between Himmelhorn and Ottohorn. What this leg actually is depends entirely on season. Early, it is a straightforward snow climb with a bit of scrambling near the top: axe, and crampons if it has firmed up. Late, the same gully is icy hardpack with choss-filled moats along the rock margins, and an overhanging boulder near the col commonly forces a loose, exposed Class 3-4 bypass on the climber's left. Coming back down late season, parties often find fixed or placed rappel anchors in the moat sections more trustworthy than downclimbing loose rock alongside hard snow - there are no bolted stations anywhere on this route, so carry slings, cord and tat to build your own.

waypoints.name: Himmelhorn Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,880 ft); from the Himmel-Otto col the route follows a ledge onto the north face and climbs the northwest side. Downclimb and rappel the same line back to the col to descend.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-32 (5.3 mi off Hannegan Pass Road); day-use fee/Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk and no potable water is available at this site.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of FS Road 32 (Hannegan Pass Road), which turns off SR 542, the Mt. Baker Highway, at about 3,100 feet. A day-use fee or Northwest Forest Pass is required at the trailhead kiosk, and there is no potable water available at the trailhead itself.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Camp
waypoints.note: Signed spur camp about a half mile below the pass with a food-storage cache and vault toilet; no reliable running water past this point.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Trail junction with the Hannegan Peak, Copper Ridge, and Chilliwack trails; leave the maintained trail here and climb the dusty gully south toward Ruth Mountain's ridge.

waypoints.name: Ruth Glacier toe / heather ridge
waypoints.note: Climbers' path skirts a minor peak on a heather-filled ridge before dropping onto the lowest snow finger of the Ruth Glacier, usually crampon-free on this well-covered lower section.

waypoints.name: Ruth Mountain summit bivy
waypoints.note: Common two-day bivy spot near Ruth's true summit (not the benchmark) before continuing to Icy Peak; flat tent sites with seasonal snowmelt for water.

waypoints.name: Ruth-Icy col descent
waypoints.note: Descend talus and snowfields off Ruth's south ridge to the saddle; avoid the steep 'death gully' variant in favor of the cairned heather slopes to climber's left.

waypoints.name: Icy Glacier crevasse traverse
waypoints.note: Rope up here to cross the Icy Glacier's northwest slope; crevasses lie mostly downhill to climber's right, so keep the rock ridge on your left.

waypoints.name: Icy Peak summit
waypoints.note: Class 4 gully with real exposure gains the summit; rappel or downclimb the same ~100 ft gully off slings around a rock horn to descend.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek trailhead (Cascade River Road mile 20)
waypoints.note: End of gravel Cascade River Road (~mile 20 from Marblemount); privy at trailhead, wilderness permit (from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center) required for overnight camping in North Cascades NP.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road from Marblemount to its end at the large gravel pullout that serves as the Eldorado trailhead, at roughly 2,100 feet. The final stretch of road is gravel, and there's a privy at the trailhead. A wilderness permit, picked up in person at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, is required for overnight camping in North Cascades National Park. Best conditions on this route typically run mid-July through early September, once the road is open and the Cascade snowpack has consolidated.

waypoints.name: Talus/boulder field entry
waypoints.note: After ~1,500 ft of forest gain the trail gives way to a cairned talus slope with cliffs on the left; stay off the climbers' path in fog, it's easy to lose in the boulders.

waypoints.name: Roush Creek Basin camps
waypoints.note: Small, level camp spots on the ridge at 6,100-6,400 ft in the basin below Eldorado Glacier; last reliable tent sites before roped glacier travel.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Glacier gain point
waypoints.note: Rope up here; snowfields lead onto the Eldorado Glacier just west (left) of the rocky ridge above Roush Creek Basin.

waypoints.name: Eldorado ice-cap / Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Common high camp on the Eldorado-Inspiration ice cap near Klawatti Col, used as the base for the traverse onto the Klawatti Glacier.

waypoints.name: Klawatti Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Stay roped crossing the crevassed Klawatti Glacier toward the base of the southeast face; open crevasses require route-finding, especially late season.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund below the southeast face
waypoints.note: A short Class 4-5 rock pitch is needed to clear the bergschrund guarding the face; a rap sling has been reported on the right (east) side for the descent moat.

waypoints.name: Klawatti Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, a rock nunatak ringed by the Klawatti, McAllister, and Inspiration Glaciers; the final few hundred feet above the schrund are 40-55° snow leading to low-5th-class rock.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the kiosk; Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required for the lot.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Established lakeshore campsites and reliable water on the east shore where Pete Lake Trail #1323 meets the lake.
waypoints.directions: Four flat, forested miles on the Cooper River Trail #1323 with barely 200 ft of gain — the easiest walking of the trip, and no measure of what follows it.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadow / PCT junction campsite
waypoints.note: Small campsite marks the Pacific Crest Trail junction; leave the maintained trail here and head west toward Lemah Meadows and the peak.
waypoints.directions: Continue along the shore past the lake camps for roughly another mile, staying left at each trail fork, to where the Pacific Crest Trail comes in.

waypoints.name: Lemah Meadows creek ford
waypoints.note: Marshy meadow crossing forces a thigh-high ford of Lemah Creek's braids, followed by roughly 1,000 ft of slide-alder bushwhacking on the meadow's northwest side.
waypoints.directions: An intermittent climbers' path with sparse cairns leads the first thousand feet or so toward Upper Lemah Meadows before fading into open ground. There is no dependable bridge over Lemah Creek, so plan on wading rather than counting on one; the braids run cold and can be thigh-deep, and with high water this is a real obstacle rather than a nuisance.

waypoints.name: Point 3854 cairn line
waypoints.note: Trail fades into brush here; sparse cairns mark the cross-country line where Lemah's five distinct summits and Whinnimic Falls first come into view.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the alder the travel goes straight up the Lemah Creek valley — a mile or two of off-trail ground past small waterfalls and pools, with several more creek crossings and further brushy stretches. Expect wet feet for the rest of the day; there is no line through here that keeps them dry. Most parties camp on a bench in the meadows near 3,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Snow gully and moat transition
waypoints.note: Prominent snow gully gains the east flank; near its top, ~200 ft of wet slabs and running water lead to a moat where snow meets rock — tricky, exposed transition onto the ledges.
waypoints.directions: Carry on up the valley beside the creek to about 5,000 ft, where the snow finger and glacier remnant begin, then take the snow itself: 35-45 degree ground where crampons and an axe are essential and the runout below is bad. Crevasses are few but they are there, so a rope team is worth having across the remnant. Start early enough that the snow is still firm — this is the section that degrades to bare ice and open moats as the snowpack goes.

waypoints.name: Southeast ridge notch
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 ledges gain the notch on the southeast ridge above 7,200 ft; the final summit scramble begins here.

waypoints.name: Lemah Mountain (Main Peak / Lemah Three)
waypoints.note: True summit of the five-tower Lemah massif, first climbed in 1923; last moves are exposed class 3-4 blocks on the summit tower.

waypoints.name: White River Campground / Glacier Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trailhead at the upper D-loop of White River Campground; NPS climbing permit and self-issue wilderness camping permit required before heading up.
waypoints.directions: From Enumclaw, WA-410 runs about 43 miles east to the park's White River entrance; turn onto the Sunrise Road, cross the White River and turn onto the White River Road, following it to the campground at the end. Sort the climbing permit and the route-specific briefing before you drive up — both are required for this line — and check the road, which is seasonal.

waypoints.name: Glacier Basin
waypoints.note: End of maintained trail in a basin below the Inter Glacier moraine; a climbers' boot track continues cross-country from here toward St. Elmo Pass.
waypoints.directions: Pick up the Glacier Basin Trail from the upper campground loop and follow it up the White River valley, about 3.5 miles and 1,500 ft, crossing the West Fork on a footbridge. It is maintained the whole way and ends in the basin. Fill everything here: this is the last dependable running water until Camp Schurman on the way out.

waypoints.name: St. Elmo Pass
waypoints.note: Saddle between Steamboat Prow and Burroughs Mountain where the Liberty Ridge approach leaves the Inter Glacier basin and drops onto the Winthrop Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends at the basin. Leave it and climb snow and scree on an unsigned boot track up to the saddle, roughly 1,500 ft above. It can be hard ice early in the season and can cornice, so have the axe and crampons where you can reach them rather than buried in the pack.

waypoints.name: Winthrop Glacier traverse below Curtis Ridge
waypoints.note: Descend from St. Elmo Pass onto the Winthrop Glacier and traverse west beneath Curtis Ridge, roped for crevasses, toward the Carbon Glacier access ramp.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the far side of the pass onto the Winthrop and rope up — roped travel with crevasse-rescue gear is the standard from here on. Contour counter-clockwise around the mountain at roughly 7,300 to 7,400 ft, crossing longitudinal crevasses and gaping moats. Rockfall comes down right where you step onto the glacier, again mid-traverse, and again at its end, so this leg wants to be moved through early.

waypoints.name: Lower Curtis Ridge / Carbon Glacier camp
waypoints.note: Standard bivy on the flat at the base of the access ramp; next day cross the crevassed Carbon Glacier, weaving through open cracks, to reach the toe of Liberty Ridge.
waypoints.directions: Carry on around the toe of Curtis Ridge to the flat ground at the edge of the Carbon Glacier, where there is room for a couple of small tents. The whole traverse sits under Willis Wall and Ptarmigan Ridge, and both throw ice and rock more freely as the day warms.

waypoints.name: Thumb Rock
waypoints.note: Rock col/campsite on the ridge crest, the usual high camp before the summit push; exposed to rockfall and wind, so many parties dig in behind the rock.
waypoints.directions: Leave early enough to have the Carbon crossing behind you before the sun is on it. Drop onto the glacier and head south toward the toe of the ridge, negotiating the cracks, then start scouting a way onto the crest at somewhere around 8,600 to 8,800 ft. From there it is 30 to 40 degree snow with scrappy scree and rock steps up to the col. The camp is exposed to wind and to anything coming off the ridge above, so build a wall and pitch in the lee of the rock.

waypoints.name: Black Pyramid
waypoints.note: Steep 40-60° ice pitches and an exposed traverse onto the ridge's east face around this dark rock buttress; a rockfall and icefall hot spot, best climbed early/frozen.
waypoints.directions: Off in the small hours. From camp, either take the short steep ice step in the middle of the rock band directly or traverse up and left around the cliff, then climb the ice gully between the rock walls, which can also be bypassed on its right. Above that the ridge steepens into sustained ice runnels. The whole stretch funnels rock and ice, so it wants to be climbed frozen and in the dark.

waypoints.name: Liberty Cap
waypoints.note: Liberty Ridge tops out on Liberty Cap's summit dome, the north sub-summit of Rainier overlooking Willis Wall; descend via the Emmons-Winthrop route past Camp Schurman.
waypoints.directions: Move out onto the east face of the ridge to get past the Black Pyramid, on exposed snow and ice up to about 60 degrees, with the angle easing back to 30 to 40 once you are around it. Several pitches of 40 to 60 degree ice and steep glacier ground then gain the Liberty Cap Glacier at around 13,500 ft. The bergschrund below the cap is usually the crux and varies year to year from a walk up a ramp to a short vertical ice step; the bridges and icy ledges across it are seasonal, so plan to climb it rather than count on finding a way over. Easier snow leads to the top.

waypoints.name: Trinity Trailhead
waypoints.note: Free self-issue wilderness permit required at the kiosk; starts the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 (Phelps Creek Trailhead, ~2 mi up Chiwawa River Road, is the alternate/nearby start named in the beta).
waypoints.directions: Trinity Trailhead is at the end of the Chiwawa River Road, Forest Road 6200, reached via Coles Corner and Highway 207 up the Chiwawa valley. Park at the road end at about 2,800 ft; the Chiwawa River Trail #1550 starts here. This is Glacier Peak Wilderness, so fill out the free self-issue permit at the kiosk before you walk away from the car. The high country beyond is typically not fully snow-free until mid-to-late July.

waypoints.name: Massie Lake junction ('M' tree marker)
waypoints.note: An 'M' with an arrow etched into a trailside tree on the left flags the unmarked, unmaintained climbers' path leaving the Chiwawa River Trail for Massie Lake.

waypoints.name: Chiwawa River ford
waypoints.note: Unbridged crossing of the Chiwawa River right at the junction; can run thigh-deep and swift during early-season snowmelt, best done early morning when flows are lowest.

waypoints.name: Massie Lake
waypoints.note: Two established fire-ring campsites on the lakeshore with good fishing and reliable water, reached via a steep, poorly-marked boot path of about 2 miles from the river ford.

waypoints.name: Ridge gain off the Massie Lake High Route
waypoints.note: Leave the Massie Lake High Route (which traverses east below the ridgecrest toward Buck Pass) and climb heather benches and talus onto Massie's west ridge.

waypoints.name: Massie Peak summit
waypoints.note: Broad rocky high point (7,534 ft on the USGS Suiattle Pass quad, listed as 'Massie Ridge' by ListsOfJohn) above Massie Lake and Buck Creek Pass; Class 2-3 scrambling along the final ridge.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Gate at the end of Mountain Loop Highway pavement; Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk before walking the closed Monte Cristo roadbed.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at Barlow Pass, at the end of the paved Mountain Loop Highway, where a gate blocks the old Monte Cristo Road. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and there is a self-issue wilderness permit kiosk at the gate before you start up the closed roadbed. The road and its river bridges beyond the gate are washed out, so nearly every current party bikes or hikes the first four-plus miles along the South Fork Sauk River to the old townsite, walking bikes through one or two washed-out sections.

waypoints.name: Weden Creek/Gothic Basin trail junction & South Fork Sauk ford
waypoints.note: Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail 724 forks right just before the road reaches the South Fork Sauk River, which must be forded or crossed on a nearby log; stay on the roadbed toward Monte Cristo.
waypoints.directions: Walk or bike the gated, washed-out Monte Cristo roadbed about a mile south from Barlow Pass, following the South Fork Sauk River; the grade is flat and easy, and rideable in dry conditions.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo townsite
waypoints.note: Old mining ghost town at the end of the roadbed; cross the South Fork Sauk on the footbridge here, established camping among the historic structures, and pick up the Glacier Basin Trail near the old USFS cabin.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the old road for roughly three more flat miles up the South Fork Sauk to the ghost town at about 2,800 ft, crossing the river on a couple of cable/suspension bridges en route. Road and bridge washouts mean most parties on bikes walk them through one or two short sections.

waypoints.name: Glacier Falls
waypoints.note: Prominent multi-tier cascade on Glacier Creek about halfway up the Glacier Basin Trail; reliable water but the trail turns steep, rocky and root-choked above and below it.
waypoints.directions: Walk past the old cabins, cross the bridge over 76 Creek, and follow "Dumas Street" through the settlement to pick up signed Glacier Basin Trail #719. The first half-mile follows an old mining road grade along Glacier Creek, then the tread turns steep, eroded and hands-on-rock as it climbs toward the falls. Glacier Creek is reliable water but drains historic mine workings — treat it, and note the elevated arsenic/heavy-metal readings, worst in the lower reaches near the townsite.

waypoints.name: Glacier Basin
waypoints.note: Open basin below the peak with established sites on Ray's Knoll and Mystery Hill; campfires banned here and within 1/4 mile, and this is the last reliable water before the col.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing the steep, slick, root-braided rock steps above the falls; the trail crosses into the Henry M. Jackson Wilderness and skirts the northeast edge of Mystery Hill before levelling out into the basin at about 4,500 ft, roughly 2.5 miles from the townsite. This section is notably harder and more slip-prone descending than ascending.

waypoints.name: North Col
waypoints.note: Gain the col via steep talus/snow (to ~45 degrees) from Glacier Basin; a moat at the col can widen badly late-season, sometimes making the step across intimidating or impassable.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends at the basin. Leave it and climb open talus and typically persistent steep snow — up to about 45 degrees for a few hundred vertical feet — up the centre gully directly toward the obvious col on Monte Cristo's north ridge, with the Wilmans Peaks and Wilmans Glacier close overhead to climber's right. An ice axe and comfort on steep firm snow are essentially mandatory into midsummer; start early so the snow is still firm.

waypoints.name: Summit chimney
waypoints.note: Short bolted chimney (5.6/5.2/5.6, ~30-75 ft) breaching the summit cliffs south of the col; old slings and a rusty piton mark it, helmet mandatory for rockfall from parties above.
waypoints.directions: Cross the moat at the col, then contour south (climber's left) across snow or talus below the summit cliffs, scouting for the obvious break/gully in the rock that gives the easiest way up to the base of the chimney.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit; from the top of the chimney it's straightforward scrambling to the register.
waypoints.directions: Climb the short bolted chimney — three moves of roughly 5.6, 5.2 and 5.6 — then from the bolted rappel anchor about 25 ft above its start take the steepish 3rd/4th-class ramp leading left, where snow whales can slicken the slabs. Above that it is Class 3-4 scrambling on loose red volcanic breccia; the final 200 ft is the worst rock on the route, so keep helmets on.

waypoints.name: Kindy Creek Road (FR-1570) Pullout
waypoints.note: Drive 14.2 mi up Cascade River Road from Marblemount, then right on FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road) to a small pullout just past the wooden bridge over Kindy Creek; Northwest Forest Pass needed to park.
waypoints.directions: From Marblemount, drive 14.2 miles up Cascade River Road, then turn right onto FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road) and park at the small pullout just past the wooden bridge over Kindy Creek, at about 1,850 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass is needed to park here. FR-1570 is washed out, so this is as far as you drive and the trip begins on foot up the blocked, brushy roadbed. Do not plan on the Green Mountain Trailhead approach instead: FR 26, the Suiattle River Road, is closed to all motor vehicles at milepost 4 by a roughly 75-ft-deep washout, under a Forest Service closure order in effect until January 1, 2028.

waypoints.name: FR-1570 Road End
waypoints.note: The old roadbed peters out here after about 2 mi of walking; leave it and drop into timber to pick up the Kindy Creek drainage upstream.

waypoints.name: Kindy Creek Crossing
waypoints.note: Last easy, reliable water before the bushwhack steepens toward the cirque — top off here.

waypoints.name: Kindy Creek Cirque
waypoints.note: Open heather basin below Buckindy's north face used as a base camp by parties traversing the Buckindy Range; flat tent sites, exposed to weather.

waypoints.name: Kindy/Goat Creek Glacier Toe
waypoints.note: Rope up here for the crevassed Kindy/Goat Creek glacier ice that guards the upper mountain.

waypoints.name: Upper Glacier Crevasse/Moat Band
waypoints.note: Open crevasses and a moat can bar direct access to the summit rocks late season; probe and stay roped through this band.

waypoints.name: Mount Buckindy Summit
waypoints.note: Class 4 summit block tops out here; the descent reverses this same downclimb back onto the glacier.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: Trailhead on SR 20 near milepost 134 (~14 mi east of Newhalem); Northwest Forest Pass needed for parking, trail drops steeply toward Ross Lake.
waypoints.directions: Reach the Ross Dam Trailhead at Happy Flats on SR-20 near milepost 134, about 14 miles east of Newhalem, at roughly 2,150 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here.

waypoints.name: Ross Lake Put-in (foot of Ross Dam Trail)
waypoints.note: Trail bottoms out at the lakeshore, losing ~500 ft in 1.3 mi; meet the Ross Lake Resort water taxi (reserve in advance) or launch a packraft/canoe here for the crossing to Big Beaver.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Landing
waypoints.note: Water taxi/paddle drop-off roughly 4.6 mi up-lake from Ross Dam, at Ross Lake's full-pool elevation; start of the Big Beaver Creek Trail through ancient redcedar groves.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Established NPS backcountry campsite on Big Beaver Creek about 11.5 mi up the trail from the landing; last reliable flowing water and flat tentsites before leaving the maintained trail.

waypoints.name: Access Creek / Big Beaver Creek Ford
waypoints.note: About a mile past Luna Camp an unmaintained, orange-flagged climbers' path forks off and fords Big Beaver Creek through dense devil's club and alder; the crossing is unbridged and can run thigh-deep.

waypoints.name: Access Basin
waypoints.note: Steep, brushy mile-long climbers' path gains roughly 1,500 ft from the creek ford to a talus/heather basin at 4,300 ft, the standard high camp for the Access Creek approach.

waypoints.name: Luna Pass (via Access Col)
waypoints.note: A steep scree chute gains Access Col at 6,100 ft, then notoriously steep heather and talus slopes lead to Luna Pass near 7,200 ft, the usual base camp for the summit push.

waypoints.name: East Fury Summit
waypoints.note: Gained via a Northeast Ridge rock scramble around a knob (broad ledge traverse), a steep descending ramp to a snow saddle, then the Southeast Glacier (30-40°, steepening near 50° at the top); descend the same glacier's true right side.

waypoints.name: Staircase Ranger Station / North Fork Skokomish Trailhead
waypoints.note: Olympic National Park wilderness permit required, booked through Recreation.gov - there are no longer paper self-registration permits at trailheads. The park entrance fee applies to park here; no Northwest Forest Pass is needed on National Park land.

waypoints.name: Spike Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp along the North Fork Skokomish River Trail on gentle old-roadbed grade; common first-night option or rest stop before the Flapjack Lakes Trail turnoff.

waypoints.name: Madeline Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Creek with small waterfalls crossed on the Flapjack Lakes Trail; last reliable water before the final steep push to the lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Black and White Lakes Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed fork just below Flapjack Lakes where the Black and White Lakes trail splits off; stay left/straight for Flapjack Lakes.

waypoints.name: Flapjack Lakes basin
waypoints.note: Established Olympic NP backcountry camp (permit + $8/person/night, no fires); standard overnight staging spot for the Lincoln scramble.

waypoints.name: Saddle below Lincoln's north sub-peak
waypoints.note: Off-trail climb from Flapjack Lakes gains this saddle on Sawtooth Ridge; route-finding is tricky here and GPS tracks tend to drift in the boulder/brush terrain.

waypoints.name: Chockstone gully / ridge scramble section
waypoints.note: Steep (35-40+ degree) loose scree and a chockstone-choked gully with Class 3+ exposed, no-fall moves; both sides of the ridge here are steep enough to slide.

waypoints.name: Mount Lincoln
waypoints.note: True summit of Mount Lincoln, second-highest point on Sawtooth Ridge; nearby North Peak (5,690ft) and Southwest Peak (5,486ft) are separate sub-summits.

waypoints.name: Gated Bridge Trailhead (FR 38 / Weyerhaeuser Rd 9000)
waypoints.note: Park at the yellow gate just before the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack (reached via Mosquito Lake Rd from Acme, then FR 38/Dailey Quarry Rd); gate is usually closed and the landowner (Hampton Family Forests) requires a paid recreation permit — bike or hike the logging roads from here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Mosquito Lake Road from Acme or Welcome to the bridge over the Middle Fork Nooksack River, then continue on Forest Road 38. Park at the yellow gate just before the bridge, at around 1,200 feet — the gate is usually closed and the landowner (Hampton Family Forests) requires a paid recreation permit. The road beyond is private timberland and access can change from year to year, so confirm the gate status before your trip.

waypoints.name: Dailey Prairie road-to-trail transition
waypoints.note: Logging roads climb roughly 2,000 ft over the first 5 miles to Dailey Prairie, a wet clearcut-plateau meadow, where the singletrack climbers' trail for the West Ridge route branches off the road.

waypoints.name: Fire ring / treeline
waypoints.note: Switchbacking trail through old logging spurs reaches treeline near 4,100 ft, marked by a firepit and cairn; bikes are left lower, where road riding ends around mile 5, and from here the path continues on foot up onto the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Katie Gap
waypoints.note: Notch where the cairned crest route dead-ends at cliffs; climbers drop through this gap to bypass the obstacle — the route's well-known routefinding crux, easy to miss in poor visibility.

waypoints.name: Summit headwall scramble
waypoints.note: Final stretch of sustained Class 3, locally Class 4, scrambling on grippy but exposed orange dunite (olivine); loose blocks and multiple false summits above this point.

waypoints.name: North Twin Sister summit
waypoints.note: True north summit of the Twin Sisters Range; broad views of Mount Baker, the San Juan Islands, and across the connecting ridge to South Twin (7,000+ ft).

waypoints.name: Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required; cross the bridge over the Middle Fork Snoqualmie River and turn right (west) onto the Pratt Connector Trail.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Middle Fork Snoqualmie Trailhead, the large lot at the end of FR 56, at about 1,040 ft. A Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee is required to park. This is a long car-to-car day with about 5,200 ft of gain, so most parties are pulling out of the lot around 5 a.m. to keep daylight in hand.

waypoints.name: Rainy Creek bridge / climbers' path split
waypoints.note: About a half mile along the Pratt Connector, cross the sturdy bridge over Rainy Creek, then peel off onto the unsigned, unmaintained Rainy Creek boot path that switchbacks away from the connector.

waypoints.name: Rainy Creek
waypoints.note: The climbers' path hugs the creek's west bank for most of the ascent to the lake — treat as the last reliable water before the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Blowdowns and talus on Rainy Creek path
waypoints.note: Unmaintained, often-faint boot path crosses several blowdowns and straight-up talus fields; easy to lose the tread in fog, dusk, or fresh snow.

waypoints.name: Rainy Lake
waypoints.note: Lake basin sitting directly beneath Preacher Mountain's exposed rock face; last flat, established camping before the ridge scramble starts at the outlet.

waypoints.name: 5,200 ft tarn / open bowl
waypoints.note: From the lake outlet climb the east-west ridge as it curves south to a small tarn in an open bowl; traverse the bowl's north side to gain the ridge leading toward the summit.

waypoints.name: Saddle below the summit ridge
waypoints.note: Broad saddle with brush, talus, and a few cliff bands to work around; spring ascents have reported cornices overhanging the east side near here.

waypoints.name: Preacher Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit reached via a short south ridge walk from the saddle; broad top with views of Rainier, Baker, and Glacier Peak.

waypoints.name: Slate Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Second switchback on the Slate Peak spur above Harts Pass, below the road's gated end; the Slate Pass Trail drops from here to the Robinson Creek (Middle Fork Pasayten) Trail #478 in the Pasayten Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Berk Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Low point of the Robinson Creek/Middle Fork Pasayten valley where the Berk Creek Trail forks north toward Freds Lake and Freds Pass; expect heavy blowdown on this stretch even by Pasayten standards.

waypoints.name: Freds Pass
waypoints.note: 7,100-ft pass gained via the Berk Creek Trail, dividing the Berk Creek and Eureka Creek drainages — the key navigation point of the cross-country approach.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Pass bench
waypoints.note: Roughly half-acre bench just southwest of 7,487-ft Shellrock Pass, the standard staging camp used for Ptarmigan and the other Pasayten Eleven summits.

waypoints.name: 7,800-ft tarn, Ptarmigan south slopes
waypoints.note: Small tarn reported reliable into late season — the last dependable water before the final summit push.

waypoints.name: South ridge gain point
waypoints.note: Leave the tarn basin and scramble cross-country over talus onto the crest of Ptarmigan's south ridge.

waypoints.name: Ptarmigan Peak
waypoints.note: True summit (8,614 ft per recent lidar survey); Class 2-3 talus and short rock steps for the final stretch, with views across the remote Pasayten Eleven.

waypoints.name: Reynolds Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Spur 4435-015 off FR 4435, which turns off Twisp River Road (~18.3 mi from Twisp); a self-issue wilderness permit is typical at the kiosk, but no Northwest Forest Pass is required at this unimproved trailhead.

waypoints.name: South Fork Reynolds Creek confluence
waypoints.note: Trail opens up where the South Fork joins the Main Fork; cross on a log and stay climbers-right of the South Fork to avoid extra creek crossings and heavy log-hopping.

waypoints.name: Trail's end / off-trail turn
waypoints.note: Reynolds Creek Trail fades into deadfall and brush here; leave it near the creek and start climbing steep, brushy slopes toward the upper basin — mark this spot, it's easy to miss on the descent.

waypoints.name: Upper Reynolds Creek basin
waypoints.note: Open basin below Reynolds' east face where trees give way to scree and talus; last flat ground and reliable creek water before the summit push.

waypoints.name: Reynolds-Rennie saddle
waypoints.note: Unnamed saddle/ridge crest between Reynolds and the Rennie/Camel's Hump massif; loose sand, scree and talus underfoot on the final approach to it.

waypoints.name: Summit block gully
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 gully splits the summit block to a notch in the ridge crest; loose, sometimes snow-covered rock with real exposure — the crux of the standard route.

waypoints.name: Reynolds Peak (true/south summit)
waypoints.note: True summit is the south horn; the lower North Peak (8,384 ft) sits about 0.3 mi north across the notch.

waypoints.name: West Fork Buttermilk Creek Trailhead (Trail #411)
waypoints.note: Vault toilet and stock loading ramp at the trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park, and Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness rules apply once you enter the wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: From Twisp, follow the Twisp River Road about 10.7 miles and turn left onto Buttermilk Creek Road, crossing the Twisp River. Stay left onto East Buttermilk Road (Forest Road 43) and follow it roughly 4 miles, then turn right onto the Road 500 spur and follow it about 2.7 miles to the West Fork Buttermilk Creek trailhead at about 3,960 ft. There is a vault toilet and a stock loading ramp at the trailhead; a Northwest Forest Pass or Interagency pass is required to park, and Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness rules apply once you cross the boundary on Trail #411.

waypoints.name: West Fork Buttermilk Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Creek crossing has been rerouted to a downed log about 100 ft upstream of the original ford after trail damage; last easy, reliable water for several miles.

waypoints.name: Sub-alpine larch stand below Fish Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Trail breaks out of burned forest into the lowest larches on the route, roughly two miles below the pass; open going but watch for deadfall from the old burn.

waypoints.name: Fish Creek Pass
waypoints.note: High point of the maintained trail (Trail #411 tops out here); first clear view down to Star Lake and the Star Peak massif opens up.

waypoints.name: Star Lake
waypoints.note: Standard basecamp for Star, Courtney, Buttermilk, Grey, and Oval Peaks; camp at least 200 ft from the lake edge per wilderness regulation.

waypoints.name: Notch west of Point 7912
waypoints.note: Climber's path switchbacks up terrible scree from the Star Lake basin to this notch; from here the route turns north onto Star Peak's west/SW ridge.

waypoints.name: SW ridge talus and scree slog
waypoints.note: Extended rock-hopping through large, unstable talus to gain the summit ridge; not technical but tedious and twisted-ankle terrain, worse if wet or snow-covered.

waypoints.name: Star Peak
waypoints.note: True summit and high point of Sawtooth Ridge; easy scrambling with hands and feet on the final approach, broad views across the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small pullout on WA-20 near milepost 126.8-127; no day-use pass required, but overnight climbers must get a backcountry permit at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center.
waypoints.directions: The Pyramid Lake Trailhead is an unmarked gravel pullout on the north shoulder of WA-20, about 21 miles east of Marblemount and 6.4 miles past Newhalem, just west of Diablo Dam near milepost 126.8-127 and around 1,130 ft. It is a small pullout with no facilities noted and no day-use pass required. Overnight parties do need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit, picked up at the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center on the way in.

waypoints.name: Pyramid Lake
waypoints.note: End of the maintained NPS trail (2.1 mi, ~1,500 ft gain); pick up the unmaintained climbers' boot path around the lake's east shore into steep brush and talus.

waypoints.name: East ridge traverse below Pyramid Peak
waypoints.note: Climbers' path gains the ridge crest above the lake then traverses, mostly on snow, below Pyramid Peak's steep east-face cliffs toward the Colonial Glacier.

waypoints.name: Colonial Glacier moraine-lake camp
waypoints.note: Flat bivy area on rock/snow beside the glacier's expanding moraine-dammed lake (formed mid-1990s) with running meltwater; standard base camp for the Snowfield/Colonial/Neve group.

waypoints.name: Colonial-Neve Glacier col
waypoints.note: Rope up here; gain the saddle via ~30-degree snow skirting the moraine lake, then drop about 200-250 ft on the far side onto the Neve Glacier.

waypoints.name: Neve Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Open crevasses scattered across the glacier's east side; stay roped and pick a middle line — turning up too early forces rock scrambling, too late puts you under cliff bands.

waypoints.name: Glacier rim turn below Horseman's Pack
waypoints.note: Break off the Snowfield approach westward along the Neve Glacier's rim, pass Horsemans Pack and The Horseman staying near the ice edge to avoid steep snow, then turn north for The Needle's southeast ridge.

waypoints.name: The Needle
waypoints.note: Sharp spire at the glacier's west edge; easy glacier travel and exposed scrambling lead to one unavoidable low 5th-class move — rappelling the final ridge is standard for the descent.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake / Yellow Aster Butte Trailhead
waypoints.note: On FR 3065 (Twin Lakes Road), 4.5 mi up from SR 542, where the road continues about 2 rough miles to Twin Lakes; Northwest Forest Pass required and roadside parking along the switchbacks is very limited.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Signed fork below Gold Run Pass: right climbs over the pass and drops to Tomyhoi Lake, route stays left toward Yellow Aster Butte meadows.
waypoints.directions: Start on the Yellow Aster Butte trail and climb steeply — roughly 1,500 ft in the first mile and a half — through an avalanche path and then forest, crossing a couple of small seasonal creeks low down that are the easiest water on the route early in the season. At the signed fork the right branch carries on over the pass and down to Tomyhoi Lake; stay left for the Yellow Aster meadows.

waypoints.name: Yellow Aster tarns / meadows
waypoints.note: High plateau of small glacier-carved tarns; all camping must be at or beyond this point (LNT-only, camp on snow/rock/bare ground, not the fragile meadow turf) — reliable water from the tarns.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the fork the grade eases and the trail traverses the south flank of the butte for a bit over two miles as the terrain opens into meadow. At an unsigned junction around three and a half miles the path to the butte's summit goes right; drop left instead on narrow, steep switchbacks into the tarn basin.

waypoints.name: Boot path onto Tomyhoi Arm
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here and pick up the well-defined climbers' boot path heading north along the crest of Tomyhoi Arm toward the southeast ridge.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the basin and head north-northwest, over a broad hump and down to a col near 6,270 ft, where a well-beaten climbers' boot path picks up along the crest. Getting onto the right crest is the thing to be careful about here — the arm runs north toward the peak, and the trail system does not go that way.

waypoints.name: Moat below Tomyhoi Glacier remnant
waypoints.note: Shallow moat/hard snow between rock and the shrinking glacier remnant — usually the crux; carry an ice axe, and it can be bypassed 100-200 ft lower via a rock finger if snow is firm.
waypoints.directions: Follow the boot path up the broadening ridge, and where the crest narrows above roughly 6,800 ft drop onto the broad benches on the north side rather than staying on top. The path fades into scree and talus as you near the toe of the glacier remnant; traverse along its upper edge to get past several rock pinnacles, assessing the ice before committing to it. Cross the moat between rock and ice — it is hard snow more often than not, which is why an axe belongs on this route, and if it is too firm it can be turned a hundred feet or two lower on a finger of rock.

waypoints.name: Notch below the false summit
waypoints.note: Gain this notch via a V-shaped Class 3.5 slot (some parties belay it), then traverse a ledge west to a wide corner leading up to the false summit.
waypoints.directions: Above the moat, gain the notch through a V-shaped slot of about Class 3.5. It is short but steep and exposed enough that parties often put a rope on it, and it is distinctly harder to reverse than to climb. From the notch, traverse a ledge west to the wide corner that leads up to the false summit.

waypoints.name: Tomyhoi Peak
waypoints.note: Class 3 scramble on solid rock from the false summit to the true summit block; sweeping views of Mt. Baker, Mt. Shuksan, and north into Canada.
waypoints.directions: From the false summit the true summit looks worse than it is. Downclimb loose ledges to the col between the two, then scramble the summit block on solid, glacier-polished rock — Class 3, with a short gabled section of ridge where the exposure is real on both sides. This is out-and-back ground, so everything climbed here has to be reversed on tired legs.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Gated Monte Cristo Road begins here (open to foot/bike only); Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required at the self-issue kiosk.

waypoints.name: Weden Creek (Gothic Basin) Trail 724 junction / South Fork Sauk River crossing
waypoints.note: Just before the river, the Weden Creek/Gothic Basin trailhead splits off; the Sauk crossing here has no bridge (log crossing only), so many day hikers turn back at this point.

waypoints.name: Monte Cristo townsite
waypoints.note: Old mining townsite with an established 6-site Forest Service campground; surface water in the area can contain arsenic and heavy metals from old tailings, so treat or pack water.

waypoints.name: Glacier Falls slick-rock section
waypoints.note: Past the townsite the Glacier Basin Trail turns very steep, climbing wet, slick bedrock alongside Glacier Falls — poor footing, especially descending in the wet.

waypoints.name: Mystery Hill camp (Glacier Basin)
waypoints.note: Established campsites on the timbered knoll of Mystery Hill (site of old Pride of the Mountains/Mystery mine adits) mark the basin high point where the maintained trail effectively ends.

waypoints.name: Dividing ridge / col below the Wilmans Spires
waypoints.note: Leave the basin and climb steep, very loose talus (or snow early season) to the col on the dividing ridge between Glacier Basin and Seventy-Six Basin; loose rock is the main hazard on this section.

waypoints.name: Wilmans Peak (summit)
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 scramble gains the true summit from the dividing ridge; first climbed 1970 via the northwest ridge, with exposed but solid rock on the final pitch.

waypoints.name: Thirtymile Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass and a free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit are required at the trailhead kiosk; no potable water on site.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Thirtymile Trailhead, at the end of West Chewuch Road, about 29 miles north of Winthrop. A Northwest Forest Pass and a free self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit, available at the trailhead kiosk, are both required, and there is no potable water on site. The road in and the high country beyond often don't fully clear of snow until late June or early July, so plan an early-season trip accordingly.

waypoints.name: Campsite below Tungsten Creek ford
waypoints.note: Established campsite on the Chewuch River roughly a quarter-mile before the Tungsten Creek ford — the last sheltered camp before the crossing.

waypoints.name: Tungsten Creek ford
waypoints.note: Unbridged, knee-deep, fast-flowing ford of Tungsten Creek; a genuine hazard during snowmelt or after rain, best crossed early in the day.

waypoints.name: Tungsten Creek Trail #534 junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Chewuch Trail #510 here onto Tungsten Creek Trail #534, climbing away from the river through young lodgepole regrowth from the 2001 burn.

waypoints.name: Tungsten Mine Camp / Boundary Trail #533 junction
waypoints.note: Site of the defunct early-1900s tungsten mine — two collapsed buildings and brick mill remnants remain; meets Boundary Trail #533 here.

waypoints.name: Boundary Trail bend toward Apex Pass
waypoints.note: Boundary Trail bends south toward Apex Pass here; leave the trail and head off-trail north/northeast up Wolframite's broad, gentle west slopes (Class 2).

waypoints.name: Wolframite Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit on open talus/tundra; broad views over the Pasayten Wilderness backcountry and Canadian border peaks.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass/Interagency Pass honored in the lot; fill out the free self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.

waypoints.name: Pete Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water and established shoreline campsites on the north side; the last easy water before the PCT junction.

waypoints.name: PCT Junction near Lemah Meadows
waypoints.note: Pete Lake Trail meets the PCT here; turn north toward Lemah Meadows rather than continuing to Spectacle Lake.

waypoints.name: Avalanche path at Chimney Creek confluence
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT at the first switchback in this avalanche path; a faint, sometimes flagged climber's path drops to a log crossing of the creek and is easy to lose in fog or low light.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Knob
waypoints.note: Standard 2-3 day basecamp on a knob just below the moraine overlooking the falls, roughly 6 hours' hike from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Chimney Glacier bergschrund/moat
waypoints.note: A short pitch of hard ~45-degree glacier ice and a bergschrund/moat crossing guard the base of the East Face; crampons and axe required, and the moat widens as the season progresses.

waypoints.name: Chimney Rock, Main (Central) Summit
waypoints.note: True summit, topped out via 3 pitches of 5.3 rock above the moat; descend via rappels and 3rd-class downclimbing back to the glacier.

waypoints.name: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; road-end parking at the top of FR 2860-120 where a dirt berm blocks further vehicle travel.
waypoints.directions: From US-101 near Sequim, follow Palo Alto Road to Lost Mountain Road (Forest Road 2870), then continue onto Forest Road 2860-120 and drive it to its end. The road stops at a dirt berm that blocks further vehicle travel, at roughly 3,300 feet, where there is room to park. A Northwest Forest Pass is required.

waypoints.name: Feeder creek crossing
waypoints.note: Small creek crossing roughly 200 yards below the unmarked trail junction — last reliable water before the dry ridge climb to Baldy.
waypoints.directions: Lower Maynard Burn Trail #816 leaves the road-end berm along an old roadbed and crosses the creek almost straight away. This is the last easy, dependable water for a long stretch, so fill up here before the climb.

waypoints.name: Ridge crest gained
waypoints.note: The climbers' boot path fades and tops out on Gray Wolf Ridge's open crest here; navigation shifts from trail-following to ridge route-finding.
waypoints.directions: Past the crossing the trail narrows to single-track and turns relentlessly steep, gaining roughly 3,000 ft in a little over two miles of fall-line tread with essentially no switchbacks. In places it is barely a boot-width across eroded, crumbly ravine crossings and slopes of packed dirt and shattered shale — a climber's path, not a graded trail. It tops out on the saddle between Tyler Peak and Baldy, where a short, steep side path drops off the crest to a snowmelt spring, the last dependable water on the route.

waypoints.name: Point 6537 (false summit below Baldy)
waypoints.note: Rocky gendarme/false summit marked on maps as Pt. 6537 — Class 2 scramblers typically skirt it on the south side rather than climb straight over.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle turn northwest onto the open ridge crest; navigation shifts from following tread to reading the ridge, so have a map or GPS out. The rocky gendarme ahead is normally skirted on its south side rather than climbed straight over.

waypoints.name: Baldy summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Baldy; the route turns and continues northwest along the open ridge crest toward Gray Wolf Mountain.
waypoints.directions: Rejoin the crest beyond the gendarme — a sign in the saddle marks the Olympic National Park boundary — and walk up the far side to Baldy's top. This stretch is straightforward going on packed dirt and shattered shale, with no scrambling.

waypoints.name: Loose scree/talus saddle
waypoints.note: Steep, loose scree and talus dropping roughly 600 ft off Baldy's north side before Peak 7076 — trekking poles recommended, exposed to wind and fog.
waypoints.directions: From Baldy the route continues northwest and immediately drops about 600 ft off the north side on steep, loose scree and talus, where poles earn their keep. The crest is fully open here and exposed to wind and to fast-moving cloud, so fix the line of the ridge in your mind before committing to the descent.

waypoints.name: Peak '7076' false summit
waypoints.note: Prominent false summit often mistaken for Gray Wolf Mountain from below; the ridge crest continues north over loose talus to the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Climb back out of the saddle and up the crest over loose talus to the prominent bump ahead. Staying close to the ridgeline is generally the cleanest way through the scree. From below this bump reads as the summit, but the crest keeps going north.

waypoints.name: Gray Wolf Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,218 ft), the highest point in Clallam County; views to Vancouver Island, Mt. Olympus, Baker, Rainier, and Glacier Peak.
waypoints.directions: Continue north along the crest over the last of the talus, detouring briefly around the occasional gendarme, and finish with a short class 2-3 scramble on loose rock to the true summit. North-facing gullies on this final stretch can hold steep snow into July.

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass (or $5/day) required at the kiosk; trail #833.2 heads south along the Dungeness River.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 2870, at about 2,880 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass, or the $5/day fee, is required at the trailhead kiosk, where Trail #833.2 begins south along the Dungeness River.

waypoints.name: Camp Handy
waypoints.note: Established riverfront meadow camp with a cedar shingle shelter; easy water access from the Dungeness River (boil/filter before drinking).

waypoints.name: Boulder Shelter
waypoints.note: Most reliable water source on the trail and the Constance Pass Trail #893 junction; sits at the foot of an avalanche chute with snapped trees in the scar.
