waypoints.name: Buckhorn Wilderness / Olympic National Park boundary
waypoints.note: Trail becomes noticeably less maintained past this boundary, with brush closing in from both sides.

waypoints.name: Home Lake
waypoints.note: Alpine lake camp walled in by Mount Constance and Warrior Peak; established sites along the west shore, base camp for the Fricaba scramble.

waypoints.name: Constance Pass
waypoints.note: High saddle giving the first clear look toward Mount Fricaba and Deception Basin; leave the maintained trail here to gain the southwest ridge.

waypoints.name: Southwest ridge scree slopes
waypoints.note: Fricaba is composed of extremely shattered, loose shale; expect tedious, ankle-turning scree on the ridge approach to the summit block.

waypoints.name: Mount Fricaba
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 summit block with views across Deception Basin to Mount Deception and Mount Mystery; descend the same southwest ridge back to Home Lake.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Northwest Forest Pass/day-use fee kiosk at the road end beside Twin Lakes; the last ~2 miles of FS-3065 below it are rough and need a high-clearance vehicle.
waypoints.directions: Drive Twin Lakes Road (FS 3065) past the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and up the final, roughly two-mile rough section to the road end at Twin Lakes, where a Northwest Forest Pass or the day-use fee is needed. The road is snow-gated through winter and spring. That last section is steep and rutted and needs a high-clearance vehicle, so many parties park at the Yellow Aster Butte trailhead and walk it.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp at the alpine lake basin between Winchester and Bear Mountains; last reliable water before the high traverse to Low and High Passes.
waypoints.directions: The lakes lie at the road end, in the basin between Winchester and Bear Mountains. Fill water here. These lakes are the last reliable source before the high traverse to Low and High Passes, and there is nothing dependable past High Pass in late season.

waypoints.name: Low Pass
waypoints.note: Trail contours Winchester Mountain's east shoulder and drops through Low Pass before climbing again toward High Pass; boot path is easy to lose here in fog or lingering snow.
waypoints.directions: From the lakes follow the Winchester Mountain Trail (#685) about half a mile to a signed junction. The left branch climbs to the Winchester lookout, so take the right fork onto the High Pass Trail (#676). It runs through meadows across Winchester Mountain's east shoulder and crosses an avalanche chute where steep, exposed snow can hang on into August, then reaches the notch of Low Pass. Carry an ice axe and know how to use it while that chute still holds snow, and expect to lose the boot path through the pass itself in fog or lingering snow.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: Basin-facing pass with the first close views of Larrabee's south face; leave the maintained High Pass Trail here and traverse cross-country toward the peak.
waypoints.directions: Climb again out of Low Pass on the High Pass Trail, a little over half a mile and about 300 feet of gain, passing the tailings and ruins of the old Gargett Mine just below the pass. High Pass is a scenic but wind-exposed spot with the first close look at Larrabee's south face. It is also the end of the maintained trail.

waypoints.name: South Ridge crossing / SW Face gullies
waypoints.note: Boot up ~40-degree scree/snow slopes to cross the south ridge onto the southwest-face gully system; Larrabee's rock is notoriously loose and crumbly, so a helmet is essential.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and follow the unmarked climbers' path as it contours and drops 100 to 200 feet northwest into the basin under Larrabee's south face, passing a small cliff band near 6,400 feet. Cross boulder fields and then scree and dirt, booting up steep ground to the southwest spur at about 6,900 feet. Cairns mark parts of this but they sit far apart and the way trail vanishes for long stretches, and boot paths here can pull you toward the East Ridge, so hold to the south and southwest side of the peak.

waypoints.name: Mount Larrabee Summit
waypoints.note: True summit (7,865 ft), 1.4 mi south of the Canada–US border; descend by reversing the south ridge/gully system back through the scree basin to High Pass.
waypoints.directions: From the spur, find the gully system cut into the rock face: two narrow parallel channels about thirty feet apart, of which the right-hand one is the line. It starts tight and opens into broken rock, Class 3 to 4 on loose phyllite, and holds steep snow into July and sometimes August. Climb it one person at a time with helmets on, since anything knocked loose runs straight down onto whoever is below. It tops out on the crest of the south ridge; follow the crest to the summit, favoring the west side and the firmer rock of the rib over the gully floor, with a faint way trail and scattered cairns coming and going.

waypoints.name: Hoh River Trailhead (Hoh Rain Forest Visitor Center)
waypoints.note: Overnight wilderness permits must be reserved in advance — none are issued at the trailhead kiosk by the visitor center; NPS entrance fee applies.

waypoints.name: Five Mile Island
waypoints.note: Trail stays nearly flat along the Hoh River through old-growth rainforest with frequent side-creek water access.

waypoints.name: Elk Lake camp
waypoints.note: Reservable backcountry camp with privy and bear wire; last reliable easy water before the trail climbs steeply to Glacier Meadows.

waypoints.name: Glacier Meadows high camp
waypoints.note: Old ranger-station camp near timberline; no camping is permitted between here and the Blue Glacier moraine.

waypoints.name: Top of Blue Glacier lateral moraine
waypoints.note: Way trail tops the moraine; the scree descent onto the ice is steep, loose, and washed out — watch for rockfall while dropping onto the glacier.

waypoints.name: Blue Glacier crossing to Snow Dome
waypoints.note: Rope up here — the glacier is riddled with crevasses and icefall; Snow Dome is the broad basin where the Olympus (east) and Mount Tom/White-Hubert Glacier (west) lines diverge.

waypoints.name: White/Hubert Glacier traverse to Tom-Olympus col
waypoints.note: Continue roped travel across the crevassed White/Hubert Glacier along the base of the Olympus massif to gain the col below Mount Tom.

waypoints.name: Mount Tom summit
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 scramble up from the col; westernmost 7,000+ ft summit in the contiguous US, with the White Glacier visible falling away below.

waypoints.name: Park Butte Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FS Road 13; a recreation pass is required to park and is not sold at the lot, so buy it ahead or pay by phone; start up Park Butte Trail 603.
waypoints.directions: Reach the Park Butte Trailhead at the end of Forest Service Road 13, via the Baker Lake Highway and the Sulfur Creek Road turnoff. Park at the trailhead lot; a recreation pass is required and is not sold on site, so buy it ahead or pay by phone. No wilderness permit is needed.

waypoints.name: Sulphur Creek crossing, Schriebers Meadow
waypoints.note: Ford Sulphur Creek on a log/plank crossing at the edge of Schriebers Meadow, then turn north toward Railroad Grade; last reliable running water before high camp.

waypoints.name: Railroad Grade Trail 603.2 junction
waypoints.note: Park Butte Trail splits here; leave it for Railroad Grade Trail 603.2, which climbs directly onto the crest of the lateral moraine.

waypoints.name: Sandy Camp
waypoints.note: Terminus of Railroad Grade Trail and the standard high camp for the Easton Glacier route; last established, durable tent sites before glacier travel.

waypoints.name: Easton Glacier toe / rope-up point
waypoints.note: Rope up for glacier travel here; head northwest toward the crater rim, weaving around open crevasses and snow bridges on the lower Easton Glacier.

waypoints.name: Sherman Crater rim / Sherman Peak spur
waypoints.note: Sulfur smell from active fumaroles vents near the crater rim; a short spur off the main Easton Glacier line leads to the Sherman Peak high point instead of continuing to Grant Peak.

waypoints.name: Sherman Peak summit
waypoints.note: False-summit high point on Mount Baker's crater rim, just south of and lower than the true summit (Grant Peak, 10,781 ft).

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Old Goodell Creek logging road on SR 20 across from Newhalem Campground; NPS backcountry permit (fee charged mid-May to early October) required for any overnight camping in North Cascades National Park.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to Newhalem. Coming from the west through Marblemount and Concrete the road is open year-round, since the seasonal highway closure gate sits farther east near Ross Dam and Diablo. Park at the Goodell Creek trailhead on the north side of SR-20, across from Newhalem Campground: take the left just past the Goodell Creek crossing, continue past the gravel pit, and follow the road to its end by the creek at about 500 ft. Any overnight camping in North Cascades National Park needs a backcountry wilderness permit, which carries a fee from mid-May to early October, and the Crescent/Terror Creek approach is usually not snow-free and reliably passable until mid-to-late July.

waypoints.name: Climbers' Path Cairn
waypoints.note: Cairn marking where the unmaintained Terror Basin/Barrier climbers' path leaves the overgrown Goodell Creek roadbed and turns steeply uphill toward the Southern Pickets.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek Log Crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Terror Creek on a large logjam ford point used by climbers approaching the Barrier; can be slick and the log position shifts year to year.

waypoints.name: The Barrier Crest
waypoints.note: Small saddle atop a notoriously loose class-3 ridge dividing the Terror and Crescent Creek basins; careful route-finding and rockfall awareness needed here.

waypoints.name: Stump Hollow
waypoints.note: Open, gentle slabby/heather basin between the Barrier and Chopping Block ridge — a common high camp for the South Route, closer to the peak than Terror Basin.

waypoints.name: South Face Gully
waypoints.note: Loose gully on the south side of the Chopping Block/Barrier ridge gains the sloping south face; helmet on, watch for rockfall onto climbers below.

waypoints.name: The Chopping Block
waypoints.note: True summit (6,819 ft), labeled Pinnacle Peak on USGS maps; visible from the North Cascades NP Newhalem visitor center on clear days.

waypoints.name: Canyon Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue free Pasayten Wilderness permit at the trailhead register; $5 day-use/Northwest Forest Pass required for the SR-20 lot near Granite/Canyon Creek.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Canyon Creek Trailhead on SR-20, roughly 16 miles west of Rainy Pass at about 1,900 feet. The lot takes a $5 day-use fee or a Northwest Forest Pass, and there is a register at the trailhead where you self-issue the free Pasayten Wilderness permit. If you are camping, the high camps fall inside the North Cascades park complex and Ross Lake NRA backcountry, so arrange a wilderness camping permit before you leave. The route is usually climbed August into September.

waypoints.name: Jackita Ridge Trail / Crater Lake Trail fork
waypoints.note: Trail #738 switchbacks ~3,400 ft in 4 miles (about 55 switchbacks) to this fork; leave Jackita Ridge Trail and go left for Crater Lake.
waypoints.directions: Cross Canyon Creek on the log-and-plank crossing right at the start; it can wash out in high water, so check its condition before committing to the trip. Above it the trail settles into roughly fifty switchbacks and about 3,400 ft of forested climbing over four miles. Carry water from the creek, because the hillside above holds none.

waypoints.name: Crater Lake
waypoints.note: Grade flattens around 5,000 ft at the lake basin; campsites sit on the rocky south lip and the outlet is the last reliable water before cross-country travel toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: Bear left at the fork and contour about a mile into the lake basin, losing a little height as the grade finally eases — the only downhill on the way in.

waypoints.name: Crater Mountain south saddle
waypoints.note: Cross-country ridge-gain point above Crater Lake where the trail ends and the route drops off-trail toward the Jerry Glacier remnant.
waypoints.directions: Pick the trail back up above the lake and grind out roughly 2,200 ft of long, hot, exposed switchbacks with no water on any of them. Somewhere around 6,700-7,200 ft leave the maintained tread and traverse off toward the gap between Crater Mountain's main summit and its east peak. Most parties are a little over four hours from the car when they reach it.

waypoints.name: Jerry Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Small crevassed glacier below the saddle; rope up or wear crampons to descend safely toward Jerry Lakes.
waypoints.directions: From the saddle the route goes downhill onto the ice on the far side. Early in the season the glacier is snow-covered and crevassed enough to justify a rope and crampons; by late summer it is often patchy or nearly bare, which makes the crossing simpler but the consequences of a slide worse.

waypoints.name: Jerry Lakes / Crater Creek Meadows camp
waypoints.note: Established bench camp near Jerry Lakes reached roughly 8-8.5 hrs from the trailhead; standard bivy for a South Face summit push the next morning.
waypoints.directions: Continue down off the ice into the lakes basin, losing around 800 ft over heather, slabs and boulders with no set line to follow. Fill water at the lakes: this is the last of it before the face.

waypoints.name: Hidden chimney / red gully, South Face
waypoints.note: Class-3 hidden chimney cuts the lower cliff band above a fish-shaped snowfield and a slinged rappel boulder; loose rock, a short rappel, and exposed steep snow through here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the heather shelf out of the basin and through the notch just south of the lakes, then climb easily to a level shoulder on the southeast ridge near 7,200 ft. From there make a rising traverse on scree westward beneath the face to the snow patches under its lower cliff band, often moving in the shallow moat where the snow has pulled away from the rock. Those snowfields are steep enough to want crampons late in the season, and the break in the cliff band above them stays hidden until you are almost underneath it.

waypoints.name: Jack Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a notch just west of the summit blocks followed by a short, exposed class-3 finish.
waypoints.directions: Above the cliff band the face gives 400-500 ft of class 3 ramps and ledges strung together by harder class 4 steps and traverses, then eases into straightforward scrambling and a band of scree beside a snow patch that returns you to the southeast ridge near 8,600 ft. Traverse and drop slightly to get in under the summit cliffs, then take the partly snow-filled gully above at class 3 and 4 with one step that can feel low fifth. Holds pull off freely on all of it, so keep the party spread sideways rather than stacked in the gully.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 7601 past Eightmile Lake; self-issue day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk, Northwest Forest Pass required for parking.
waypoints.directions: The Stuart Lake Trailhead sits at the end of Eightmile Road (FR 7601), which leaves Icicle Creek Road (FR 7600); follow FR 7601 to its end, past Eightmile Lake. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park in the lot. Fill out the self-issue day-use wilderness permit at the kiosk before you start walking.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake Trail junction
waypoints.note: Continue straight on the Stuart Lake Trail past this junction, staying along Mountaineer Creek rather than turning left for Colchuck Lake.

waypoints.name: Off-trail turn toward Stuart Glacier basin
waypoints.note: About a mile past the Colchuck junction, leave the maintained trail and follow the valley climbers' path up toward the Sherpa/Stuart Glacier basin — often snow-covered and poorly marked March-June.

waypoints.name: Basin below Sherpa Glacier
waypoints.note: Standard base camp for the Stuart Glacier Couloir in a small flat valley at the base of the Sherpa Glacier, about 5 miles and 5+ hours from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Stuart Glacier Couloir bergschrund
waypoints.note: Bergschrund at the couloir's entrance around 7,800 ft is often the route's crux obstacle; parties have belayed across on sugary, unconsolidated snow.

waypoints.name: West Ridge notch (col)
waypoints.note: Couloir tops out at this notch on the West Ridge, the col shared with the West Ridge route, after a narrow ice/snow section that can run 40-60 degrees; continue over mixed 5th-class rock toward the summit.

waypoints.name: Mount Stuart summit
waypoints.note: True summit, typically reached via 2-3 short pitches of mid-5th-class rock above the West Ridge notch.

waypoints.name: FR-1570 Washout Parking (Cascade River crossing)
waypoints.note: Small pullout for 4-5 cars just past a washed-out culvert, 0.4 mi beyond the Cascade River bridge and 1.9 mi off Cascade River Road (FR-15) at mile 14.2 from Marblemount; FR-1570 is impassable to vehicles beyond here.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road roughly 14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn onto FR-1570, signed for Kindy Ridge and Found Lake, crossing the Cascade River. Park at the washout just past the washed-out culvert — a small pullout with room for four or five cars at about 1,250 ft. FR-1570 is impassable to vehicles beyond this point and the old spur is permanently closed, so the hike starts on the abandoned roadbed near Vee Creek. Cascade River Road access is seasonal and typically gated in winter, and mid-July through September is when the lower slopes are clear enough to be worth the drive.

waypoints.name: Overgrown Roadbed / Way-Trail Start
waypoints.note: The abandoned FR-1570 roadbed (brushy, several windfalls to step over) ends at the edge of an old clearcut where a steep, unmarked way-trail breaks off uphill toward Kindy Ridge.

waypoints.name: Way-Trail Knoll / Kindy Ridge Gain
waypoints.note: The steep boot path tops out on a knoll where the route gains the Kindy Ridge crest; footing is loose and the path is easy to lose in fog or low visibility.

waypoints.name: Kindy Ridge Climbers' Boot Path
waypoints.note: Point on the shared Kindy Ridge climbers' route used by Snowking/Buckindy parties; Mutchler's approach breaks off the ridge here toward Cyclone Lake basin rather than continuing toward Found Peak.

waypoints.name: Cyclone Lake Basin
waypoints.note: Largest and highest of the alpine lakes on Snowking's flanks; established rough campsites on the benches above the lake serve as the usual base camp for Mutchler's summit push, with reliable water from the lake and inlet tarns.

waypoints.name: Heather/Rock Flank Below Summit Block
waypoints.note: Loose, exposed heather-and-rock slope gaining Mutchler's upper flanks — the Class 3 crux referenced in the route grade; can be slick when wet and is the same terrain used on descent.

waypoints.name: Mutchler Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at 7,150 ft; open views west to Snowking Mountain's glaciers and south/east across the Buckindy group peaks (Sonny Boy, Bruseth, Misch, Buckindy).

waypoints.name: Eagle Creek/Oval Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue Northwest Forest Pass / $5 day-use fee at the kiosk; trail enters Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness a short way in, vault toilet and stock ramp at the lot.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Eagle Creek/Oval trailhead at about 3,000 ft, at the end of FR 4420-080. Reach it on Twisp River Road/FR 44 roughly 12.5 miles west of Twisp, then turn up the West Buttermilk/FR 4420 spur and follow it to the road's end. There is a vault toilet and a stock ramp at the lot; self-issue a Northwest Forest Pass or pay the $5 day-use fee at the kiosk, and the trail enters the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness a short way in. The access road and the lake basins are typically snow-free from early July into October.

waypoints.name: Eagle Creek / Oval Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Ford the side stream here, then turn left off Eagle Creek Trail #410 onto Oval Creek Trail #410A toward the Oval Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Oval Creek / Oval Lakes Trail junction
waypoints.note: Bear onto Oval Lakes Trail #410B, which climbs past an old moraine below Gray Peak before dropping into the Oval Lakes basin — this section burned in the 2018 Crescent Fire and is dry/dusty with little shade.

waypoints.name: Middle Oval Lake outflow
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends at the lake outflow; established stock/backpacker camp with fishing (cutthroat) — this is where you leave the trail and start up open heather/talus toward the Sawtooth crest.

waypoints.name: Saddle on Oval Peak's south ridge
waypoints.note: Gain the Sawtooth crest via open heather and talus above the lake's outflow; no maintained tread here, easy to lose the line in fog or low visibility.

waypoints.name: Talus/boulder field on the south ridge crest
waypoints.note: Broad ridge of loose, sometimes slick talus and large boulders — the crux annoyance of the route (twisted-ankle terrain, not technical).

waypoints.name: Oval Peak
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Lake Chelan-Sawtooth Wilderness and of the Methow Mountains; small rock glacier on the north slopes, views of Star, Courtney, and Gray Peaks.

waypoints.name: White River Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 6400; Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee required, self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From Coles Corner on Highway 2, take Highway 207 toward Lake Wenatchee, then follow White River Road (Forest Road 6400) to its end at the White River Trailhead, at about 2,300 feet. The road has a repeated history of flash-flood washouts, so it's worth checking current conditions before you commit to the drive. At the trailhead, a Northwest Forest Pass or day-use fee is required, and you self-issue a Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Boulder Creek crossing / Boulder Pass Trail junction
waypoints.note: White River Trail crosses Boulder Creek and passes the Boulder Pass Trail junction; well-traveled tread ends and maintenance gets sparser beyond here.

waypoints.name: Old camp at Thunder Creek
waypoints.note: Established campsite next to the Thunder Creek crossing at the point where an old sheepherders' path leaves the White River Trail toward Thunder Basin.

waypoints.name: Slide alder bushwhack
waypoints.note: Dense slide alder choking the old trail up to about 5,000 ft — the most difficult route-finding and bushwhacking on the approach.

waypoints.name: Thunder Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Open basin with granite slabs and small tarns below Tenpeak's south side; standard high camp for the Southeast Route, with views of Glacier Peak and Clark Mountain.

waypoints.name: Notch/col east of the summit block
waypoints.note: Reached by crossing talus and a snowfield (crampons useful) from Thunder Basin; described by climbers as an 'incredibly windy notch' below the east face.

waypoints.name: Loose gully and broken chimney
waypoints.note: Southeast-trending gully with loose, wobbly rock leads to a ledge system, then a broken chimney with a jam crack (Class 4/low 5th) — watch for rockfall onto party below.

waypoints.name: Tenpeak Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit of Tenpeak Mountain on the Chelan/Snohomish county line; reverse the chimney, gully, and col to descend.

waypoints.name: Obstruction Point Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the 8-mile Obstruction Point Road off Hurricane Ridge; a wilderness permit reserved in advance (there is no self-registration here) and a bear canister are required; canisters are loaned at the Wilderness Information Center in Port Angeles.

waypoints.name: Lillian Ridge crest
waypoints.note: Grand Pass Trail crests this narrow, wind-exposed ridge with steep drop-offs into the Badger and Lillian River valleys on either side.

waypoints.name: Gladys Lake
waypoints.note: Small subalpine lake roughly 1.5 miles and 1,000 ft below Grand Pass; treat before filling, it's the last reliable water before the final push to the pass.

waypoints.name: Grand Pass
waypoints.note: High alpine col dividing the Grand Valley/Lillian Ridge drainage from Cameron Creek; trail turns south here and drops into Cameron Basin toward Cameron Pass.

waypoints.name: Cameron Pass
waypoints.note: Highest trail-served pass in Olympic National Park; the north-facing approach holds snow into late July/August and NPS advises carrying an ice axe for self-arrest.

waypoints.name: Upper Cameron Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Established high camp in the Cameron Creek/Lost Basin area beyond the pass; bear canister required (trees too short to hang food) and notoriously buggy in season.

waypoints.name: Mount Claywood Summit
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scramble up open talus slopes from the high camp; cairns mark the easiest line through occasional Class 3 steps to the true summit.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.directions: Drive to Leavenworth and head up Icicle Creek Road, then turn onto Forest Road 7601 (signed as Eightmile Road) and follow it to its end, around 3,540 feet, where the Stuart Lake Trailhead and the Stuart/Colchuck Lake Trail begin.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead on Cascade River Road (23.1 mi gravel from Marblemount); NPS wilderness permit required for camps beyond Cascade Pass.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the very end of Cascade River Road (FR-15), about 23.1 miles of gravel road from Marblemount, at roughly 3,600 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park here. Overnight parties also need a North Cascades backcountry camping permit for Kool-Aid Lake, picked up in person in Marblemount before you drive out.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Maintained trail tops out here; leave it for the unmaintained climber's path bearing SSE toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: The Cascade Pass Trail is well-graded and heavily switchbacked the whole way, 3.7 miles and about 1,700 ft to the notch between Mixup Peak and Cascade Peak. It melts out by early to mid summer and is the busiest stretch of the trip, since it is a popular day hike in its own right. Nothing here needs route-finding; the work starts at the pass.

waypoints.name: Cache Glacier toe / Mixup Peak traverse
waypoints.note: Rising traverse on snow or heather across Mixup Peak's east flank to the base of Cache Glacier; isolated crevasses and firm morning snow can require an axe.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the pass and pick up a climber's path bearing south-southeast, making a rising traverse across open heather and snow benches on Mixup Peak's east flank. The path is intermittent and vanishes entirely under early-season snow, so this is where navigation starts to matter. It brings you to the toe of the Cache Glacier around 6,000 ft, where firm morning snow makes an ice axe worth its weight.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Glaciated gap atop Cache Glacier between Magic Mountain and Mixup Peak; descend SSE from here toward Kool-Aid Lake.
waypoints.directions: Ascend the glacier on moderate snow, steepening to about 35 degrees near the top, to reach the col. This glacier is small and generally free of significant crevasse hazard, but it is still a snow slope with runout below, so crampons are worth carrying depending on season and how firm it is.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn with established bivy sites used as base camp for the peak; outlet is snowbound and unreliable for water into early summer.
waypoints.directions: From the col the route drops rather than climbs: a climber's path makes a descending traverse to the southeast down to the lake. Do not continue north over the col. This is the last reliable water of the trip, and the outlet can still be snowbound into early summer, so fill here before going up.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain–Hurry-up Peak col
waypoints.note: Climb roughly 1,000 ft from Kool-Aid Lake to this saddle, then gain Magic Mountain's south ridge toward the false summit.
waypoints.directions: From the lake the ground turns up again onto heather and scree leading east to the saddle between Magic Mountain and Hurry-Up Peak, where the South Ridge proper begins. There is no water at all above the lake, so leave camp carrying what you need. The slope is uniform and featureless in cloud, which is the only real navigational catch on this leg.

waypoints.name: Corkscrew ledges below false summit
waypoints.note: Past the false summit, drop about 80 ft down a loose gully to exposed Class 3-4 ledges that corkscrew the east side of the peak; a hand line or short belay is often used here.
waypoints.directions: Follow the South Ridge up on heather and rock at class 3 to a false summit, roughly 50 ft below and southeast of the true one. Do not try to stay on the crest from there. Drop about 50-80 ft down a loose, dirty gully on the far side to reach the ledge system, which is the technical crux of the whole outing.

waypoints.name: Magic Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit, marking the northern terminus of the Ptarmigan Traverse on the North Cascades NP / Glacier Peak Wilderness boundary.
waypoints.directions: The ledges are broken, exposed class 3-4 and corkscrew around the east side of the summit tower to the top. A hand line or a short belay is commonly used, and many parties rappel this section on the way down off a sling around a horn or chockstone, since there is no fixed hardware on this summit. Fresh snow can force a detour through the moat, and the loose rock means this section bites harder on the descent than on the way up.

waypoints.name: Tubal Cain Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk; trailhead reached via FR-2870, 12.5 mi past Dungeness Forks Campground.

waypoints.name: Silver Creek footlog crossing
waypoints.note: Trail crosses Silver Creek on a footlog in the forested lower section; reliable flowing water before the trail opens up.

waypoints.name: Tull Canyon Trail junction / Tubal Cain Mine
waypoints.note: Unsigned spur angles left to the 1952 B-17 crash site (0.6 mi, +450 ft); old mine adit and tailings visible on the hillside, mine-shaft water runoff is not safe to drink untreated.

waypoints.name: Buckhorn Lake spur junction
waypoints.note: Signed junction where a faint side trail drops toward Buckhorn Lake; the main Tubal Cain Trail continues on toward Marmot Pass.

waypoints.name: Buckhorn Lake basin (avalanche debris flat)
waypoints.note: Established camp area in an open flat about 200 ft above and south of Buckhorn Lake; last reliable camp/water before leaving the trail.

waypoints.name: Iron-Worthington col
waypoints.note: Off-trail brush and blowdown give way to open scree/talus gaining this saddle between Iron Mountain and Worthington; the west-side gully is the boot-ski descent route back toward Buckhorn Lake.

waypoints.name: Loose rock band below the summit plateau
waypoints.note: Notoriously rotten, loose Olympic rock on the final scramble through the rock band; test holds and watch for rockfall onto climbers below.

waypoints.name: Mount Worthington summit
waypoints.note: Flat, open summit plateau with a ~40-ft Class 3 summit block some parties rope up for; views to Rainier, Baker, Shuksan, and Puget Sound on clear days.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead
waypoints.note: Road's-end trailhead past Sol Duc Hot Springs; overnight permits are not issued here, so arrange the wilderness camping permit in advance before starting up the Sol Duc River Trail.

waypoints.name: Heart Lake
waypoints.note: Subalpine, heart-shaped lake below the High Divide reached via old-growth forest on the Sol Duc River Trail; reliable water and the last established camp before leaving maintained trail.
waypoints.directions: The Sol Duc River Trail runs nearly level through old-growth forest past Sol Duc Falls, then climbs steadily through the subalpine meadows of Sol Duc Park to the lake basin. It is maintained tread the whole way, roughly eight miles and about 2,800 ft of gain, so most parties treat this as a full first day under an overnight pack. Stream crossings lower on the Sol Duc can run high and cold early in the season.

waypoints.name: High Divide / Cat Basin Junction
waypoints.note: Trail junction where the High Divide Trail meets the primitive Cat Basin route; scramblers leave the maintained trail here and head cross-country toward the Bailey Range.
waypoints.directions: A short half mile of switchbacks above the lake gains about 300 ft onto the crest of the High Divide to reach the junction. It is brief, but it is the end of maintained tread — everything past this point is unmarked cross-country travel, so fix your position on the map here rather than after the tread runs out.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk (below Cat Peak)
waypoints.note: Narrow, jumbled rock arete on the ridge between Cat Peak and Mount Carrie with exposed class 2-3 moves; full packs make balance and route-finding tricky, especially in fog.
waypoints.directions: Follow the High Divide Trail east from the junction until the maintained tread ends, then pick up an obvious boot path that climbs steeply toward the ridge crest past Cat Peak. Snow lingers on these north-facing slopes into early July and an ice axe is worth carrying that early. Crossing the arete itself takes roughly 45 minutes with a full pack — the low point sits in the middle, and it is balance and route-finding on the exposed class 2-3 moves that slow parties down, not the climbing.

waypoints.name: Eleven Bull Basin
waypoints.note: Heather benches and streams gushing off the hillside beneath Mount Carrie and Ruth Peak make this the standard camp for a Ruth Peak push; no reliable water again until Cream Lake, roughly an hour further on.
waypoints.directions: There is a meltwater source at the east end of the arete, known as Boston Charlie's, worth topping off at before the traverse. From there faint herd paths sidehill below the crest, losing about 600 ft over a mile and a half through a string of gullies that need hands-on scrambling with an overnight pack. Count on one to two hours before the slope eases into the basin's heather benches and streams.

waypoints.name: Ruth Peak
waypoints.note: True summit of Ruth Peak, third-highest peak in the Bailey Range; final pitch above Eleven Bull Basin is class 2-3 scrambling with views to Mount Olympus and the Fairchild Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Leave the overnight gear at camp and climb north out of the basin on open talus and heather, gaining roughly 1,600 ft in about a mile. The terrain steepens from meadow into talus bands and gets noticeably looser near the top, but stays class 2-3 throughout. Cairns and boot paths are effectively nonexistent up here, so pick the path of least resistance and expect route-finding rather than difficulty to be the work.

waypoints.name: Upper Dungeness / Royal Basin Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large parking area at end of FR 2870 off Palo Alto Rd/FR 28; $5 NW Forest day-use fee, self-issue permit envelope, pit toilets.
waypoints.directions: Take Highway 101 to just before Sequim Bay State Park and turn onto Louella Road, then follow Palo Alto Road, which becomes Forest Road 28, for about 6 miles. Turn right on FR 2880 along the Dungeness River, and 1.7 miles later turn left on FR 2870 and stay on it for roughly 6.5 to 9 miles of gravel that winds steeply down to a river crossing. It ends at the large Dungeness/Royal Basin trailhead lot, with a picnic table and a vault toilet. There is a $5 Northwest Forest day-use fee, paid with the self-issue permit envelope at the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Royal Creek / Dungeness River crossings
waypoints.note: Trail parallels and repeatedly crosses Royal Creek on log bridges after the first easy mile along the Dungeness River; reliable water throughout.

waypoints.name: Shelter Rock
waypoints.note: Massive overhanging rock on the left just below Royal Lake, a well-known trail landmark and informal rest stop.

waypoints.name: Royal Lake
waypoints.note: Designated backcountry campsites at the outlet; overnight permit and bear canister required, no campfires.

waypoints.name: Arrowhead Meadow
waypoints.note: Trail crosses a log bridge, climbs steeply, then levels into this open alpine meadow below Upper Royal Basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Royal Basin tarns
waypoints.note: First of several milky-blue tarns fed by snowmelt off the Needles; last reliable water before the talus climb.

waypoints.name: East flank talus/scree gully below the Needles
waypoints.note: Loose, unstable talus and scree on the exposed east side; rockfall risk increases with parties above, especially in shoulder-season conditions.

waypoints.name: Sundial summit block
waypoints.note: Final class 3 scramble up a short, exposed ridge-top pitch to the true summit; loose rock and steep drop-offs on the east side.

waypoints.name: Washington Pass Hairpin Turn
waypoints.note: Parking on the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 below Washington Pass.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda / Ingalls Way Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of North Fork Teanaway Road (FR-9737); self-issue Northwest Forest Pass and Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit at the trailhead kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From I-90 exit 85, SR-970 runs about seven miles to the Teanaway Road; follow it north as it becomes the North Fork Teanaway Road and then FR-9737, the last ten miles or so unpaved. Arrive early on a summer weekend — this lot also serves Longs Pass and Mount Stuart and it fills.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Pass
waypoints.note: Ingalls Way Trail crests the pass and enters Alpine Lakes Wilderness here, with the first open view of Mount Stuart and the Ingalls Peaks; bear right toward Lake Ingalls (the left fork is the easier, more maintained option, right crosses Headlight Creek).
waypoints.directions: Three miles and around 2,300 ft on Ingalls Way #1390. A signed fork at about half a mile sends the Esmeralda Basin trail off low and left; stay right and uphill. The Longs Pass trail branches right at roughly a mile and a half; carry straight on. Above that it is steady switchbacks through open larch to the crest.

waypoints.name: Lake Ingalls
waypoints.note: Turquoise alpine tarn directly below the Ingalls Peaks and a reliable water source, but shoreline camping is discouraged/restricted to protect the fragile basin and resident mountain goats.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail drops into the basin and contours about a mile, giving back a few hundred feet, to the lake. Two tracks cross the basin and rejoin; the more maintained one avoids the Headlight Creek crossing. Fill and filter at the lake, because nothing higher holds water.

waypoints.name: North/South Peak col
waypoints.note: From the lake, climb slabs, talus and boulders following the obvious dike feature up to the saddle between North and South Ingalls Peaks, aiming just left of the small rock spire that marks the notch.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained trail at the lake and work up talus, slabs and boulders toward the saddle. An obvious dike line gives the easiest going. Aim to pass just left of the small rock spire sitting in the notch. This unmarked route-finding on loose talus is the real crux of the day for most parties, more than any single move.

waypoints.name: West-side gully below the saddle
waypoints.note: Drop about 50 ft down the west side of the ridge and pick one of several loose Class 2-3 gullies back up to the crest; lingering steep snow just below the saddle is common into midsummer.
waypoints.directions: Do not carry on straight up the crest from the col. Drop about fifty feet onto the west side and pick one of several short Class 2-3 gullies, roughly a hundred feet of loose rock, back up to the ridge. Dropping less makes it steeper, dropping more makes it easier. The west-side drop-offs are severe and steep snow often lingers just below the saddle into midsummer.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Peak - South Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, gained by a short mixed snow-and-rock ridge scramble from the gully top; Mount Stuart dominates the view east across the Ingalls Creek valley.
waypoints.directions: From the top of the gully follow the crest over blocky rock and any remaining snow, exposed but with good holds on grippy peridotite. The summit block takes one short high-Class-3 move; squeezing through the crack between blocks avoids the most exposed line. Move one at a time through the gully below, since anything knocked loose lands on whoever is beneath.

waypoints.name: High Bridge PCT/Agnes Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the Stehekin Valley shuttle road; PCT crosses High Bridge here, southbound tread starts about a quarter-mile up the road toward Agnes Creek.
waypoints.directions: There is no road connection to this trailhead from outside the valley: reach Stehekin by the Lake Chelan ferry or floatplane, then take the Stehekin Valley Road or the NPS shuttle about eleven miles up-valley to the bridge. Plan the whole trip around the boat and shuttle timetable, because missing the last run means an extra night.

waypoints.name: Fivemile Camp (Agnes Creek)
waypoints.note: First established creekside camp on the PCT south of High Bridge; reliable water from Agnes Creek.
waypoints.directions: Walk a few hundred yards up the road from the bridge to pick up the PCT heading south, then follow it into the Agnes Creek valley. The tread is well graded and gains only a few hundred feet through old-growth forest, with the gorge and its cascades off to the side for much of the way.

waypoints.name: Swamp Creek Camp
waypoints.note: PCT camp at the Swamp Creek fork; jumping-off point for the unmaintained boot path toward Needle Peak's north ridge.
waypoints.directions: Keep heading south on the PCT for roughly another three miles of easy valley walking to the fork where Swamp Creek comes in. The peak shows itself up-valley along this stretch. Most parties treat this as an overnight approach rather than pushing straight through from the boat.

waypoints.name: Boot path departure at 3,200 ft
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained Swamp Creek trail here onto a steep, brushy, unmarked boot path climbing toward the north ridge crest.
waypoints.directions: From camp pick up the unmaintained trail up the Swamp Creek drainage; expect blowdown, eroded tread and heavy brush, plus a crossing of Swamp Creek itself on a large downed log. Wasps are a recurring nuisance in this overgrown section. The path is left behind at about 3,200 ft, below the north ridge.

waypoints.name: Polished slab gully, ~5,000 ft
waypoints.note: Slick, polished slab in the gully; parties bypass west through rock with a tree belay to gain about 200 ft.
waypoints.directions: Climb straight up the steep, brushy hillside toward the ridge, roughly 1,800 ft of gain with no tread, on vegetation, dirt and small steps of rock. Higher up the ground funnels into the gully system. The slab at its head is the first place the route stops being a walk.

waypoints.name: Ridgeline camp above 5,400 ft
waypoints.note: Flat ground near the ridge crest with the first clear view of Needle Peak; no water on site, must be hauled up from below.
waypoints.directions: Do not force the polished slab directly. The usual line escapes west through the taller rock, and parties belay off a tree for roughly 200 ft to regain the top of the gully, so carry a rope for this leg. Above it the angle eases onto the crest and flat ground appears.

waypoints.name: Crux notch, 7,300-7,400 ft
waypoints.note: Exposed Class 4/5.0 notch with krummholz for holds and wobbly boulders on the ridge above; this is the section that is downclimbed or rappelled on descent.
waypoints.directions: From the camp the ridge steepens into dense krummholz and sloping slabs beneath the sheer north face; stay west of the crest and weave through the cliff bands rather than trying the face. Taking the rib immediately west of the gully gives better holds, and the two lines merge after about 600 ft of gain. Exposure above the talus field is serious through here and blocks are loose — this is Class 4 with a 5.0 move at the notch, not a walk-up.

waypoints.name: Needle Peak Summit
waypoints.note: True summit; final approach is a narrow gully with overhanging rock below the top.
waypoints.directions: Step across the notch onto the summit ridge and follow ledges just below the crest on its east side. The crest itself overhangs and is stacked with wobbly rock near the top, so the last stretch drops into a narrow gully before topping out. Study this section on the way up, because it is the piece you have to reverse or rappel coming down.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of the Cascade River Road, 23 mi from Marblemount. No parking fee here, but a North Cascades National Park backcountry permit is needed for camping inside the park on the way to Cache Col.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Top of the maintained trail and start of cross-country travel; the Ptarmigan Traverse leaves the trail here, climbing south toward Cache Glacier.
waypoints.directions: From the road-end parking, the maintained trail switchbacks up through old-growth forest for about 3.7 miles, gaining roughly 1,800 ft to the pass. This is the last of the graded trail — everything beyond is cross-country.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Gap between Magic Mountain and Mix-up Peak reached via a roped crossing of Cache Glacier; historically holds steep snow requiring careful kick-stepping into early season.
waypoints.directions: At the pass pick up the climbers' path bearing south-southeast. It makes a rising traverse across the east flank of Mixup Peak on heather and snow, crossing a spur ridge, to reach the toe of the Cache Glacier near 6,000 ft; rope up for the glacier to the col, or take the loose gully on its left. Early season the Mixup traverse is snow-covered with a poor runout, and late in the year the col itself can moat out and become awkward to step onto.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine tarn on rock slabs about a mile SSE of Cache Col; the traverse's standard first camp, with limited flat tentsites.
waypoints.directions: From the col descend and traverse south-southeast for about a mile over rock and heather-covered benches. Keep the ice axe in hand — the steep heather is the real hazard on this leg, not the snow.

waypoints.name: Middle Cascade Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Roped glacier crossing near Spider-Formidable Col with reported open crevasses on the lower icefall; parties stay high on the less-broken upper glacier and rope up, especially in whiteout or late-season bare-ice conditions.
waypoints.directions: From the lake climb to the Red Ledge, an exposed traverse across a cliff band that is the route-finding crux of this section and holds snow and ice early in the season. Above it, work up and around onto the Middle Cascade Glacier and rope up before stepping on: the lower icefall is broken and open crevasses are reported, so stay high on the less-fractured upper glacier.

waypoints.name: Yang Yang Lakes
waypoints.note: Second traditional camp on the traverse, a pair of tarns below Le Conte Mountain; reliable water but exposed, breezy campsites on heather benches.
waypoints.directions: Climb the glacier to the low gap west of Spider Mountain, then descend steep snow and scree on the far side to the tarns. In whiteout this is easy ground to get wrong — the gap is the only obvious break in the ridge.

waypoints.name: White Rock Lakes
waypoints.note: Third camp, reached via the South Cascade Glacier col and Lizard Col; base camp for the optional Lizard Mountain side-scramble on a layover day.
waypoints.directions: Climb from the lakes toward Le Conte Mountain, cross the Le Conte Glacier to the gap north of Sentinel Peak, then traverse onto the South Cascade Glacier and cross it to the col at its head. Drop the steep slopes on the far side into the lake basin. Both glaciers are roped travel, and this is the longest and most sustained day on the traverse.

waypoints.name: Lizard Mountain
waypoints.note: Class 3 south-ridge scramble on somewhat loose rock from the White Rock Lakes camp; summit gives a close-up view of the Chikamin Glacier spilling off Dome Peak.
waypoints.directions: From camp climb back out of the basin and gain the peak's south ridge. It is short but the rock is blocky and loose, up to Class 3 — keep the party out of each other's fall line rather than strung out directly below.

waypoints.name: Depot Creek Road turnout, Chilliwack Lake Road
waypoints.note: Park at the large turnout ~0.1 mi before the yellow steel bridge over Depot Creek on Chilliwack Lake Road, BC; high-clearance vehicles can continue up Depot Creek Road.
waypoints.directions: This one starts on the Canadian side. Drive Chilliwack Lake Road in BC and park at the large turnout about 0.1 mi before the yellow steel bridge over Depot Creek, around 2,040 ft; Depot Creek Road leaves here as an unsigned dirt spur. High-clearance vehicles can continue up it, but it is a rough 4WD track that ends at a major washout a short way in, where foot travel begins on the old logging-road grade. From there the old Depot Creek trail runs south into the US and the international border is crossed on foot at the obelisk and trail register, and a wilderness permit is required beyond that point for overnight stays on the US side. Target a stable window in July through September, when the crossing at Depot Creek Falls and the border-crossing road are most passable; Depot Creek runs highest with June and July snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Depot Creek Road washout
waypoints.note: Rough 4WD track ends at a major washout around 1.7 mi in; foot travel begins here on the old logging-road grade.

waypoints.name: US/Canada border marker
waypoints.note: Boundary marker and North Cascades National Park register along the climbers' path; a wilderness permit is required beyond here for overnight stays on the US side.

waypoints.name: Depot Creek Falls handline crossing
waypoints.note: Fixed handlines cross the base of Depot Creek Falls; do not attempt this crossing without them, especially when the rock is wet.

waypoints.name: Ouzel Lake camp
waypoints.note: Established bivy sites ringing Ouzel Lake, the standard base camp for Custer/Rahm/Redoubt/Spickard, with reliable water from the lake.

waypoints.name: Redoubt Glacier access / flying-buttress col
waypoints.note: Scramble the broken buttress southwest of Ouzel Lake, work right onto the Redoubt Glacier, and cross to the low point (~7,800 ft) in the rock flying buttress toward Custer/Spickard.

waypoints.name: Crux gully below Custer-Spickard col
waypoints.note: Vertical, 6-8 ft-wide rock gully that is the route's technical crux (Class 3-4, wet rock reported loose); downclimb or short-rappel here if wet or icy on descent.

waypoints.name: Mount Custer summit
waypoints.note: True summit (8,630 ft) with views across the Redoubt, Spickard, and Custer massif of the Chilliwack Group.

waypoints.name: Hairpin Turn Pullout, SR-20
waypoints.note: Large roadside pullout on the outside of the SR-20 hairpin switchback (~MP 163); no permit needed, boot path drops south into the trees toward Early Winters Creek.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR-20 to the large roadside pullout at the hairpin turn near Milepost 163, just below Washington Pass. No permit or pass is needed to park there. This is the North Cascades Highway, so the drive only exists once SR-20 opens for the season — it usually reopens in April or early May and closes again in late November or early December. From the pullout the boot path drops south off the shoulder into the trees and fords Early Winters Creek directly across from the parking area; there is no maintained trail or trail number above the highway.

waypoints.name: Early Winters Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Early Winters Creek on the climbers' path just past the pullout; can run high and fast with June snowmelt.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Pass
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' trail gains the Kangaroo Ridge crest here after ~1,500 ft of climbing through trees and the lower gully; route-finding is easy below but the path is faint near the top.

waypoints.name: Snow-filled gully below Big Kangaroo
waypoints.note: Parallel gullies angling up the west face beneath Big Kangaroo hold snow well into July; ice axe recommended for the ascending traverse.

waypoints.name: Kangaroo Ridge basin
waypoints.note: Talus basin below Big Kangaroo and Mushroom Tower where the standard route splits off toward Mushroom Tower's south side; class 3 scrambling begins here.

waypoints.name: Base of South Side route
waypoints.note: Roped low-5th-class climbing starts here; rack light with a few small cams for the step-across move higher up.

waypoints.name: Step-across move to summit block
waypoints.note: Exposed step-across move gains the blocky, semi-detached summit block; the route's crux and essentially unprotected.

waypoints.name: Mushroom Tower summit
waypoints.note: Small blocky summit; rappel begins from a fixed anchor of two old 1/4-inch bolts to reverse the ascent route.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Mine Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Forest Road 4065; follow Sunrise Mine Trail to Headlee Pass then around Sperry Peak to the Vesper/Sperry basin.

waypoints.name: Cairned pass toward Copper Lake / start of ledge traverse
North Face ledge-access notch (True Grit start)
Vesper Peak north face
waypoints.note: True Grit is a 5-pitch, 5.8 line up the north face, one of the original moderate routes on the wall.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR-20 parking near milepost 134; self-issue NPS wilderness permit required well ahead for Big Beaver/Ross Lake camps before starting.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Trail junction (via Ross Dam)
waypoints.note: Cross Ross Dam and follow the Ross Lake shoreline to the Big Beaver Trail junction; Ross Lake Resort's water taxi to Big Beaver Landing can bypass this shoreline stretch.

waypoints.name: Thirtynine Mile Creek Camp
waypoints.note: Tent sites on the west bank, stock/horse camp on the east bank of Thirtynine Mile Creek; the last reliable running water and last legal campsite before leaving the trail.

waypoints.name: Off-trail departure onto Thirtynine Mile Ridge
waypoints.note: Leave Big Beaver Trail between the creek crossing and the 'Thirtynine Mile Creek Camp' marker post, climbing north through a brushy gully and adjacent rib — reported as a horrible bushwhack low down.

waypoints.name: Point 6071, Thirtynine Mile Ridge crest
waypoints.note: Ridge crest gained here; travel eases to open Class 1-2 walking above this point after steep timber and brush below.

waypoints.name: Saddle camp below Point 6690, South Ridge
waypoints.note: Informal saddle campsite used to split the climb into two days; no running water — carry up from Thirtynine Mile Creek.

waypoints.name: Points 7361 and 7547 (false summits)
waypoints.note: Exposed rocky high points along the crest before the true summit; the descent requires down-climbing short Class 3 steps here in reverse.

waypoints.name: Mount Prophet summit
waypoints.note: True summit reached via a short Class 3 rock scramble on the final southeast ridge; exposure is present but never bad.

waypoints.name: Stafford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 9703; ~20-car lot with pit toilet, Northwest Forest Pass or $5 self-issue fee required; trail has seen closures for Labor Mountain Fire damage so check current USFS alerts before going.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Teanaway River Road to 29 Pines Campground, bear right where the pavement ends, then turn onto Stafford Creek Road and follow it a couple of miles to where it ends at the trailhead. The last stretch is dirt and washboarded but passable to low-clearance cars in dry conditions.

waypoints.name: Stafford Creek crossing, Stafford Creek Meadows
waypoints.note: Stream crossing in the meadows on Trail #1359; last reliable water before the drier climb toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Trail #1359 leaves the lot at an easy grade through dry ponderosa and lodgepole forest, staying close to Stafford Creek most of the way. A short rerouted section of steeper switchbacks near the half-mile mark bypasses old avalanche-damaged tread. The forest stays open and the grade never gets hard before the trail reaches the marshy meadow ground.

waypoints.name: Standup Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail #1359 meets the Standup Creek Trail about 2 miles below Navaho Pass; continue straight/left on #1359 toward the pass.
waypoints.directions: Stay on Stafford Creek Trail #1359, still gaining gradually along the creek, to the signed junction with the Standup Creek Trail (#1369).

waypoints.name: Upper meadow camp
waypoints.note: Established camp area in the upper meadow, about half a mile below the pass; common overnight staging spot before the steep push above.
waypoints.directions: Continue on Trail #1359 above the junction; the trail opens out into a large, marshy subalpine meadow with a feeder stream — another water source, and the usual base camp for parties splitting the trip over two days.

waypoints.name: Navaho Pass
waypoints.note: Junction with the old County Line Trail (Cascade Creek Trail #1217); barren, rocky 'moon-scape' terrain with big Enchantments views, but very exposed to wind for camping.
waypoints.directions: Above the meadow the trail leaves the trees and switchbacks up open, rocky slope for the last stretch, gaining roughly 500 ft to the saddle. There is no water and essentially no shade on this section, and on the dry east side it bakes on a warm afternoon.

waypoints.name: South ridge scramble path
waypoints.note: Steep climber's path of loose scree and dirt gaining the south ridge; snow patches can linger into July, making poles/microspikes worthwhile.
waypoints.directions: From the pass turn east and follow the crest trail a short way toward the peak, then leave it where a boot path breaks off uphill onto the south ridge. The path is loose scree over dirt and steepens quickly, so poles earn their keep and it is easy to push rock down onto anyone below you.

waypoints.name: Navaho Peak
waypoints.note: True summit at 7,223 ft on the Alpine Lakes Wilderness boundary; panoramic views of the Enchantments and Stuart Range.
waypoints.directions: Follow the crest up for a bit over 600 ft of gain on broken rock and scree; the scrambling stays easy Class 2 with hands wanted only occasionally. Stay on the ridge line rather than dropping onto the looser slopes on either side, which are steeper than they look from above.

waypoints.name: Kindy Creek Road (FR-1570) Y-junction parking
waypoints.note: From Marblemount drive 14.2 mi up Cascade River Road, cross the Cascade River on a concrete bridge onto FR-1570 (Kindy Creek Road), and park at the Y-junction; the spur beyond is rough and often blocked to vehicles.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road about 14.2 miles from Marblemount and turn right onto FR-1570, Kindy Creek Road, which crosses the Cascade River on a concrete bridge. Within roughly 0.4 mile the right fork is blocked by boulders and washout, and parking is at that Y-junction, around 1,200 ft. The spur beyond is permanently closed to vehicles by windfall, brush and washouts, so the trip opens with a two-to-three mile road walk rather than a trailhead. June through September is the working window.

waypoints.name: Blocked road ends, climbers' path begins
waypoints.note: After roughly 3 miles walking the deteriorating FR-1570 spur, an unmarked climbers' path breaks left into the trees and climbs very steeply — easy to lose, especially descending in fog.
waypoints.directions: Walk the closed roadbed uphill for two to three miles through windfall and encroaching brush; two large washouts cut it and can be awkward when snowmelt is running high. The road ends at a small clearing with an old firepit. The climbers' path leaves on the left near that clearing, unsigned and steep from its first step, so fix the spot in your mind on the way in, because it is much harder to find from above in fog on the way out.

waypoints.name: Boggy meadow low camp
waypoints.note: First flat ground with seasonal boggy water on the ridge, used by parties splitting the approach into two days before pushing on toward Found Peak.
waypoints.directions: The path climbs hard and unrelentingly, first through brush and then into old growth, on boot-beaten tread over roots and rock. There is no water on this section, so carry what you need from below. The grade finally eases at a boggy bench with room for a tent, where the water is seasonal and can be down to puddles late in the year.

waypoints.name: Found Peak saddle / Found Lake fisherman's trail fork
waypoints.note: A fisherman's trail forks west here toward Found Lake; stay on the climbers' path and traverse below Peak 5116 rather than going directly over it.
waypoints.directions: Follow the ridge up from the bench. The tread is faint through grass and boulders on this stretch and parties routinely lose it, picking it up again a few hundred feet higher; when in doubt stay on the crest. The fork sits on the saddle and is marked by a cairn rather than a sign.

waypoints.name: Cyclone Lake meadows
waypoints.note: The most established camp on the route, with reliable water and good tent sites in the meadows below Peak 5791/5860; most overnight parties stage here for the summit push.
waypoints.directions: Traverse on past the fork and continue along Kindy Ridge, dropping past the meadow that holds Found Lake and crossing the next small point to the saddle beyond. The line generally stays on the west side of the crest. Net elevation change is small but the ground rolls constantly, so it takes longer than the distance suggests.

waypoints.name: High camp on rock/snow benches
waypoints.note: Exposed benches below the Snowking Glacier used to shorten summit day; wind-exposed with limited flat tent space.
waypoints.directions: Work counterclockwise around the lake to the head of its outlet stream. A rock wall lines the east side of the outlet; drop toward the lake about fifty feet east of the stream and turn the end of the wall with a single class 3 move rather than trying to force the wall directly. From there climb the gentle granite buttress to the southwest, turning several small cliff bands above or below as they come, onto the slabs and benches.

waypoints.name: Crevassed section below the south notch
waypoints.note: The route crosses a crevassed stretch of the Snowking Glacier below the south notch — rope up and probe, particularly in late season when snow bridges are thin.
waypoints.directions: From the benches climb past the small tarns and traverse rocky slopes toward the notch, then take the short drop into the gap that puts you onto the glacier. Rope up before stepping onto the snow rather than partway across.

waypoints.name: Snowking Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via the easy east/southeast ridge with class 3 scrambling on the final blocks; broad views across the North Cascades Core.
waypoints.directions: Cross the glacier to the southwest, aiming straight at the peak, and leave the snow for rock on the left where a faint scree path picks up. The last of it is sustained class 2 boulder-hopping with a few class 3 moves on the final blocks, taken from the southeast ridge or the south slope. Time the return so you are back across the glacier before the afternoon sun softens the bridges.

waypoints.name: Washington Pass Hairpin Turn
waypoints.note: Parking on the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 below Washington Pass.

waypoints.name: Niederprum Trailhead
waypoints.note: Park at the washed-out 2008 bridge on 387th Ave NE/Old Mine Road (steel gate and boulder barricade); the old Niederprum mining-road grade climbs south from here toward Snow Gulch.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the Niederprum Trailhead on 387th Ave NE / Old Mine Road, where a steel gate and boulder barricade close the road at the 2008 washed-out Moose Creek bridge. Park at the barricade, around 900 ft; the old Niederprum mining-road grade climbs south from here toward Snow Gulch. Early-season parties leave the car pre-dawn and walk the road grade straight into the Snow Gulch approach, so budget the barricade detour into the start time rather than the drive.

waypoints.name: Creek-drainage bushwhack (~1,100-2,200 ft)
waypoints.note: Steep, brush-choked section of the drainage above the trailhead that's only reasonably passable once deep spring snow has buried the alder and devil's club.

waypoints.name: Niederprum Mine bench / traverse start
waypoints.note: Sloping bench near the old Niederprum mine workings, marked by a large broken, silvered snag; begin the rising leftward traverse toward Lone Tree Pass here.

waypoints.name: Lone Tree Pass
waypoints.note: Gain this narrow notch via a steep snowfield (crampons recommended) — the transition point from forested ridge to open alpine/glacier terrain.

waypoints.name: Whitehorse Ridge Camp
waypoints.note: Broad snow platform just beyond Lone Tree Pass with room for several tents and views from Mt. Baker to Dome Peak; the standard high camp for a two-day ascent.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: A broad snow couloir below prominent Point 6357 tops out here; this pass is the entry point onto the Whitehorse (So-Bahli-Ahli) Glacier.

waypoints.name: Whitehorse Glacier bergschrund / wind-cirque snowfinger
waypoints.note: Crevasses and a bergschrund open across the upper glacier by mid-summer near the 'wind cirque' snowfinger below the summit block; rope up and probe snow bridges.

waypoints.name: Whitehorse Mountain summit
waypoints.note: True summit, typically gained by a short roped pitch or snowfinger above the wind cirque; descent reverses the glacier and Lone Tree Pass snow slopes.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 32 (Ruth Creek Road), 5.3 mi off the Mt Baker Hwy; Northwest Forest Pass required to park, self-issue wilderness permit needed past the pass for overnight travel into North Cascades NP.

waypoints.name: Hannegan Pass
waypoints.note: Broad meadow pass on the Mt Baker Wilderness/park boundary ridge where the trail crests and then switchbacks steeply down into the Chilliwack River drainage.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Hannegan Pass Trail (#674) about 4.2 miles up the Ruth Creek valley, gaining roughly 1,900 ft through forest and avalanche meadows before switchbacks bring you to the pass.

waypoints.name: Boundary Camp
waypoints.note: First-night camp just inside the park boundary below the pass with a reliable stream for water; trail forks here toward the Chilliwack River/Copper Ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the pass the trail switchbacks steeply down the east side into the Chilliwack River drainage, losing about 1,250 ft in a mile to the camp just inside the park boundary. The stream at camp is reliable water.

waypoints.name: Chilliwack River crossing
waypoints.note: Ford (or cable/log crossing depending on season and bridge status) of the Chilliwack River; can run high, fast, and cold during snowmelt — check current NPS crossing status before counting on a bridge.
waypoints.directions: Continue down-valley on the Chilliwack River Trail, dropping about 1,500 ft over roughly five miles of forest past the Copper Creek and U.S. Cabin camps to the river. Bears have been persistent at camps in this drainage, so use hard-sided food storage anywhere you stop. Bring gloves for the hand-pulled cable car, and check current park crossing status before counting on it.

waypoints.name: Brush Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Chilliwack River Trail and turn up the Brush Creek Trail toward Whatcom Pass; junction is easy to miss in overgrown brush.
waypoints.directions: Cross the river and follow the trail about a mile up-valley past Indian Creek Camp to the signed Brush Creek junction, where the tread toward Whatcom Pass turns off. This stretch carries major blowdown from the 2021-22 fire damage, and the junction itself is easy to walk past when the brush is up.

waypoints.name: Graybeal Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp on Brush Creek that's often dry by late summer — fill water at the creek about half a mile before camp rather than counting on a source here.
waypoints.directions: Turn up the Brush Creek Trail and climb roughly 1,250 ft over about two miles toward Whatcom Pass, through the 2022 burn — expect rockfall off unstable burned switchbacks and falling snags overhead. Graybeal's own water source is often dry by late summer, so fill at the creek about half a mile below camp rather than counting on finding water at the site.

waypoints.name: Open slopes above Brush Creek (leave trail)
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail on the brushy avalanche-path slopes below Whatcom Pass and angle northwest toward Indian Mountain; no path from here, steep heather/slide-alder terrain with genuine route-finding as noted in route beta.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the Brush Creek Trail another mile and a half toward Whatcom Pass, then leave the maintained tread where the brushy avalanche paths open up below the pass. There is no path beyond this point, and the slide alder and steep heather make the route-finding genuinely sustained in both directions.

waypoints.name: Indian Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; the peak drops over 4,100 ft to the Brush Creek/Indian Creek valley in roughly a mile, and hikers viewing it from the Whatcom Pass ridge describe an abrupt cliff on its north side above Indian Creek's headwaters — stay well back from that edge.
waypoints.directions: Climb cross-country up open heather, talus and short loose rock steps, gaining roughly 2,300 ft in about a mile and a half. Nothing here needs a rope, but the peak throws over 4,100 ft down to the valley in about a mile, so the ground stays steep the whole way and there is no quicker line down — the descent reverses this one. Near the top, stay well back from the north edge, which drops abruptly to the head of Indian Creek.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead
waypoints.note: Large trailhead parking lot at the end of Sol Duc Hot Springs Road; Olympic National Park entrance pass required; overnight trips need a wilderness permit reserved in advance, since none are issued at the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Turn south off US 101 onto Sol Duc Hot Springs Road (about 29 miles west of Port Angeles) and follow it, paved the whole way, past the park entrance station, the Sol Duc Hot Springs Resort and the campground to the large lot at road's end — the trailhead is at the very end, beyond the resort.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Falls
waypoints.note: Trail crosses a footbridge just below the falls; last easy, reliable water before the climb toward Appleton Pass begins in earnest.
waypoints.directions: From the end of the lot take the Sol Duc River Trail up the valley: 0.8 mi of wide, near-level old-growth tread with essentially no elevation change (1,950 to 1,980 ft), ending at the footbridge just below the falls. This is the last easy, reliable water taken straight off the trail before the climbing starts.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass Trail junction
waypoints.note: Leave the Sol Duc River Trail here and turn right/uphill onto the Appleton Pass Trail; elevation is a rough interpolation along the NPS-stated 2,000-5,100 ft climb.

waypoints.name: Appleton Pass
waypoints.note: Broad alpine pass on the Bailey Range crest with meadows and views into the Boulder Lake basin; leave the maintained trail here to begin cross-country travel into the Bailey Range proper.

waypoints.name: The Cat Walk (Cat Peak traverse)
waypoints.note: Old, narrow, exposed use-path sidehilling the steep flanks of Cat Peak; the steepest, most exposure-prone stretch of the whole approach, worse with a full pack.

waypoints.name: Boston Charlie's Camp
waypoints.note: Small flat tent spot at the east end of the Cat Walk with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond; water needs filtering and the site is exposed to wind/weather.
waypoints.directions: Follow the sidehill path east to the far end of the Cat Walk arete, giving back roughly 200 ft. The camp is a single small flat tent spot at the east end with a shallow melt-water sinkhole pond beside it — filter that water, and expect the site to be fully exposed to wind and weather.

waypoints.name: Mount Carrie ridge/glacier gain
waypoints.note: Highest point in the Bailey Range (0.84 mi SW of Fairchild's summit); per the descent beta this is where the route regains the ridge/glacier system linking to the Fairchild Glacier.
waypoints.directions: Climb roughly 1,700 ft southeast from Boston Charlie's onto Mount Carrie (6,995 ft), the highest point in the Bailey Range. There is a real choice here: many parties sidehill the loose, exposed talus across Carrie's south face, but staying higher — up the ridge on Carrie's north side, over or just under the summit — avoids the worst of the sidehilling and sets up a cleaner entry onto the Fairchild Glacier. Where the crest becomes too sharp to walk, traverse up across the scree flanks. There is no reliable water on this stretch, so tank up at camp.

waypoints.name: Fairchild Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up and don crampons/axe here; follow the wind-formed ridge down-glacier toward the exit col on Ruth Peak's shoulder — crevasse hazard, especially late season when snow bridges are thin.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 300 ft northeast off Carrie's ridge onto the upper Fairchild Glacier, which starts around 6,600-6,700 ft on the Bailey crest and falls away to the northeast. Rope up and put on crampons here; an ice axe is wanted most of the season. Rather than taking the direct line, follow the wind-formed snow ridge running down the glacier — the same idea as the Hogsback on Mount Hood — which keeps you clear of the crevasses. Late season the snow bridges thin and the surface goes to bare, hard ice, so this is full crampon technique, not microspikes.

waypoints.name: Mount Fairchild
waypoints.note: Second-highest peak in the Bailey Range; short final scramble on snow and rock from the glacier saddle to the true summit.
waypoints.directions: Leave the wind ridge and take the steeper exit section up onto Fairchild's summit ridge: roughly 35-40 degrees of snow past an icy patch, the steepest ground on the route. Stay roped and in crampons through it. From the summit ridge a short scramble on snow and rock gains the 6,899 ft true summit, second-highest in the Bailey Range. There is no rappel anywhere on this climb — the only way off is to reverse the entire line, and the glacier softens through the afternoon, so set an early turnaround.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Cascade River Road, 23.1 mi from Marblemount; NPS backcountry permit required for overnight stays, self-issue day-use is free.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road east from Marblemount roughly 23 miles to its end at the Cascade Pass Trailhead at 3,660 ft — paved for about the first 10 miles, then good gravel the rest of the way. Check the road first: in some seasons, including 2026, vehicles are stopped at the Eldorado gate at mile 20 and the last 3 miles and 1,500 ft to the trailhead must be walked or biked. There is a parking area and a vault toilet at the road end. Day use is free and self-issue; a North Cascades backcountry permit is required for overnight camps, released seasonally through recreation.gov, and the camps along this traverse fill fast in peak season. Because the traverse exits at a different trailhead on the Suiattle River Road, most parties pre-arrange a car shuttle rather than leaving a vehicle here.

waypoints.name: Cascade Pass
waypoints.note: Trail tread ends at the pass; leave the maintained trail here and head south/southeast onto the Ptarmigan Traverse cross-country route.
waypoints.directions: The trail switchbacks around thirty times up a forested rib, gaining roughly 1,400 ft in the first two miles, then eases into a long ascending traverse through meadow and talus to the pass. Figure two and a half to three and a half hours. Snowfields can lie across the traverse well into summer.

waypoints.name: Cache Col
waypoints.note: Gap between Magic Mountain and Mix-up Peak at the head of Cache Glacier; gain it via a steep snow/scree gully, the crux route-finding point of day one.
waypoints.directions: Leave the trail at the pass and head south and east, traversing and climbing across the Mixup arm on boot path, talus and snow bands. Gain the shoulder, follow the snow ramp up, then drop onto the Cache Glacier and walk it to the col at its head. The step onto the glacier is short but steep and can be corniced, and an axe and crampons are normal here into midsummer.

waypoints.name: Kool-Aid Lake
waypoints.note: Small tarn on a bench south of Cache Col, the standard first-night bivy/base camp for the traverse; exposed, fog often wafts up from the valley below.
waypoints.directions: Descend the far side of the col — a steep snowfield that usually needs an axe and crampons well into midsummer — and lose several hundred feet to the bench holding the tarn. The runout below the snow is rocky, so this is not a place to glissade blind into fog.

waypoints.name: Red Ledge
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed rock ledge cutting west from Art's Knoll that bypasses cliffs south of Kool-Aid Lake; can hold an open moat, verglas, or fresh snow that makes the traverse 'spicy' even in summer.
waypoints.directions: Climb out of the lake basin and traverse toward the cliff band running west off Art's Knoll, which from below looks like it stops the route entirely. Getting established usually means scrambling through the moat at the snow-rock margin and up a few feet of Class 3 to reach the ledge. Once on it the ledge is broad and walkable, unless it is holding snow or verglas.

waypoints.name: LeConte Glacier
waypoints.note: Broad glacier basin below Old Guard and Sentinel Peaks; rope up here and cross to the base of Old Guard's west/northwest side, watching for late-season crevasses near the peak's flanks.
waypoints.directions: This leg is far longer than the mileage on file suggests. Past the ledge the traverse crosses the Middle Cascade Glacier, climbs to the Spider-Formidable col and drops to the Yang Yang Lakes basin, after which the ledge system known as the goat path leads up onto the LeConte snowfield and glacier. It is a full day or more of committing glaciated terrain, travelled roped and with crevasse-rescue gear, not a short hop from the Red Ledge.

waypoints.name: Snowfinger / Couloir Base
waypoints.note: Steep snow couloir (Class 2/3) rising off the glacier to the base of the summit rock; firm early-morning snow can require an axe and crampons, softening to punchy postholing by afternoon.
waypoints.directions: From the glacier work to the foot of the snow finger rising toward the summit rock and get onto it wherever the moat or bergschrund allows — that transition is often the awkward move of the day.
