It is a few hundred feet of steep snow, best taken early while it is firm, since by afternoon it softens to punchy postholing and the runout is back onto the glacier.

waypoints.name: Old Guard Peak
waypoints.note: Short Class 3 scramble up grippy gabbro from the top of the couloir gains the true summit, with views across the LeConte Glacier to Sentinel Peak and Dome Peak.
waypoints.directions: Top out of the couloir and finish on a short Class 3 scramble up blocky gabbro, a few hundred feet on rock that takes hands but stays straightforward. Stash axe and crampons somewhere you will find them again, because the descent reverses this same couloir.

waypoints.name: Goodell Creek / Upper Goodell Group Camp trailhead (SR-20, Newhalem)
waypoints.note: Unpaved turnout off SR-20 across from Newhalem, signed for Goodell Creek; no parking pass is needed, but an overnight trip needs a wilderness permit from the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is an unpaved turnout off SR-20 across from Newhalem, signed for Goodell Creek. No parking pass is needed here, but camping in the Terror or Crescent Creek basins needs a wilderness permit, issued in person at the Wilderness Information Center in Marblemount.

waypoints.name: Upper trail fork
waypoints.note: Maintained forestry-road-bed trail ends here; climbers' path continues with diminishing cairns/flagging toward Terror Creek.

waypoints.name: Terror Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Terror Creek at a shallow braid; crossing depth is very flow-dependent and can be a wade in high water.

waypoints.name: The Barrier
waypoints.note: Steep, brushy, loose ridge (spur off Mt. Degenhardt) separating Terror Creek and Crescent Creek basins; cross via a loose ledge system near the lower Terror Glacier or a higher moat crossing below Degenhardt — classic sustained 'Pickets Class 3' that turns parties back.

waypoints.name: Crescent Creek Basin camp (below Mt. Terror)
waypoints.note: Established high camp on a flat bench below Mount Terror with meltwater from two overhead slab streams; the basin runs 6,050–6,440 ft.

waypoints.name: Eye Col gully traverse
waypoints.note: Drop ~300 ft below the moraine to Crescent Creek's head, then rising-traverse below the Eye Col gully past an adjacent buttress on a minor rib to a notch, avoiding a closed chimney and loose choss.

waypoints.name: West Twin Needle
waypoints.note: Above the Eye Col, a 5.7 pitch up white slabs on the east face, then scrambling to the true summit; descend via rappels off the Himmelhorn–West Twin Needle col.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the standard Southwest Buttress; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf shared with the standard Southwest Buttress route.
waypoints.directions: From the lot, walk about 90 feet back down the road and look for the log or clump of trees spanning the river; cross there, then head roughly 100 feet away from the water to pick up the climbers' path and turn upstream on it. The path climbs steeply through forest and talus into Eldorado Basin and on up to the Inspiration Glacier shelf, about 5,500 ft of gain to camps near 7,400-7,600 ft.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Crossing point from Inspiration Glacier onto the McAllister Glacier, shared with the standard buttress approach.
waypoints.directions: Rope up at camp and cross the Inspiration Glacier northeast to the low point on the divide. The ground is otherwise gentle; crevasses are the only real difficulty.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Shared approach point; the Direct variant departs the standard buttress line higher on the wall, not at the base.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the col onto the McAllister Glacier and work down and across it, keeping to its skier's right where the ice steepens and breaks up, then traverse toward the pass.

waypoints.name: Direct Southwest Buttress topout
waypoints.note: Harder direct start (5.10a) rejoins the standard buttress line before the final corner to the summit ridge.
waypoints.directions: About 700 vertical feet below the pass, start up the prominent gully running to the base of the buttress; it usually holds snow year-round. Rope up before its top, because the moat guarding the base of the rock can open into a deep, exposed gap. From the gully exit do not traverse right onto the standard 1985 line: carry straight on up two direct pitches of 4th and low-5th scrambling to three vertical cracks, take the rightmost at about 5.8 into the strenuous 5.10 crux and mantel onto a large bench, then follow awkward 5.8+ ground toward the large white slabby rock where the original route comes back in.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: True summit shared with the standard Southwest Buttress finish.
waypoints.directions: From the junction with the 1985 line, blocky mid-5th rock and a final corner lead onto the summit ridge, then a short scramble along it gains the true summit.

waypoints.name: Thornton Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Thornton Lakes Road (FR 1470) off SR-20 near milepost 117; Northwest Forest Pass and a self-issue wilderness permit are needed for overnight camps.

waypoints.name: Thornton Creek hanging meadow
waypoints.note: Trail crosses Thornton Creek in a ferny hanging meadow below talus; leave the maintained trail here to begin cross-country travel through steep timber.

waypoints.name: Thornton Ridge
waypoints.note: Rocky shoulder where the route breaks out of slide-alder thickets and thick cedar-limb brush onto the open ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Thornton Pass (camp knob)
waypoints.note: Flat benches on the crest are the standard base camp, reached roughly 7-8 hours from the trailhead.

waypoints.name: Triumph Pass
waypoints.note: Breezy saddle linking Mount Triumph and Mount Despair with a north-facing snowfield just below; cross here to drop into the Despair Lakes basin.

waypoints.name: Lake Regret
waypoints.note: Frequently still partially frozen in season; go around the west side rather than crossing the ice.

waypoints.name: Upper Despair Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water source and scenic rest/turnaround point in the Despair Lakes basin below the southeast face.

waypoints.name: Mount Despair summit
waypoints.note: Gained via short roped Class 3-5 pitches up the southeast-face cliff band, finishing with an exposed Class 5.0 dihedral to the summit block.

waypoints.name: Nooksack Cirque Trailhead (Trail #750)
waypoints.note: Ford Ruth Creek on a log right at the trailhead — no bridge; a crossing that's dry in the morning can be thigh-deep by afternoon in summer.
waypoints.directions: From Bellingham, take Interstate 5 to the Sunset Drive/Mount Baker exit and follow the Mount Baker Highway (WA-542) east through Glacier, the last place to resupply groceries, to the Nooksack River bridge about 13 miles past town. Turn left onto Nooksack River Road (Forest Service Road 32) immediately before the bridge, staying left at 0.5 miles and right at 1.4 miles from the highway. The road washes out at 2.3 miles; park there at Ruth Creek, about 2,156 feet, since the road is not drivable beyond that point. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit is required for overnight stays: $10 per person plus a $6 reservation fee, reserved on Recreation.gov. In-person pickup is at the Glacier Public Service Center on Thursdays and Fridays in season; a walk-up can be requested by email the morning before.

waypoints.name: Off-trail ford of the Nooksack River
waypoints.note: Leave the Nooksack Cirque Trail here (flagged but easy to miss) and drop steeply to ford the Nooksack before climbing the forested ridge toward Price Lake.

waypoints.name: Price Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water at the lake outlet; the boot path climbs the ridge along the lake's north side up onto the moraine above.

waypoints.name: Moraine bivy at ~5,900 ft
waypoints.note: Last reliable flat rock for bivy bags before the tower, with a gentle slope leading directly onto the Price Glacier.

waypoints.name: Price Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Rope up and cross the crevassed lower Price Glacier toward the tower's base; move fast — the traverse sits under rockfall-prone slopes off the tower's north face.

waypoints.name: Steep snow/ice gully
waypoints.note: 50°+ snow/ice gully funnels rockfall from above; climb it early in the day before the sun loosens debris.

waypoints.name: Nooksack Bivouac saddle
waypoints.note: Flat, often snow-covered col between the tower and the connecting ridge; used as a high bivy and as the rappel-anchor point on the descent.

waypoints.name: Nooksack Tower summit
waypoints.note: Small, exposed summit block with a brass Mountaineers register and loose rock near the top.

waypoints.name: Beverly Turnpike Trailhead
waypoints.note: Shared trailhead with Bean Creek Basin at the end of the rough, overgrown FR 9737-112 spur road.
waypoints.directions: From the North Fork Teanaway River Road, turn onto the FR-9737-112 spur and follow it to its end at the Beverly Turnpike trailhead, around 3,650 ft. The spur is rough and overgrown, and the gravel access opens with spring snowmelt; that plus the Ingalls Creek ford further along makes July through September the practical window. It is the shared lot with Bean Creek Basin, so at about half a mile bear left onto signed Trail #1391 rather than taking the Bean Creek fork, which is a commonly reported mistake here.

waypoints.name: Beverly Creek Trail (FST 1391) / Fourth Creek Trail (FST 1226.1) junction
waypoints.note: Faint fork in forested/open terrain; bear toward Fourth Creek Trail for the pass rather than continuing up Beverly Creek.

waypoints.name: Fourth Creek Pass
waypoints.note: Low, treed pass on the drainage divide reached via a steep final 0.3-mile push; descends into the Fourth Creek drainage on the far side.

waypoints.name: Fourth Creek / Ingalls Creek confluence camp
waypoints.note: Established basecamp near the creek confluence used by most south-side parties before the summit push.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Creek ford
waypoints.note: Potentially dangerous ford — cold and swift in early season, can be partially frozen with slick ice-covered rocks.

waypoints.name: South-side gully, west of the main gully
waypoints.note: Class 2 scrambling up loose rock in the gully just west of Argonaut's main south gully, heading for the summit ridge.

waypoints.name: Argonaut Peak summit (west summit, true)
waypoints.note: Final moves onto the true (west) summit ridge are harder than the class 2 approach suggests, often low class 3/4.

waypoints.name: Smithbrook Trailhead
waypoints.note: Small dirt lot (~15 cars) off FR 6700; no parking pass required, no potable water or restrooms.
waypoints.directions: Drive US 2 to the Smithbrook Road turnoff, Forest Road 6700, about 4.2 miles east of the Stevens Pass summit — roughly half a mile east of milepost 69 if you are coming from the Leavenworth and Wenatchee side, or about 68 miles out from Everett and Seattle. Follow FR 6700 about 2.7 to 3 miles to the Smithbrook Trailhead at around 4,000 feet, on the left. The gravel road is normally passable to passenger cars once it is snow-free, but it is not plowed in winter; then you park at a pullout on the highway shoulder and add miles of road travel each way. The trailhead is a small dirt lot for about 15 cars, with no potable water and no restrooms.

waypoints.name: Rainy Creek tributary crossing
waypoints.note: Only reliable stream on this route — top off here, nothing higher on the ridge.

waypoints.name: Union Gap - PCT junction
waypoints.note: Smithbrook Trail #1590 switchbacks up old growth to this saddle and ends at the PCT; leave the maintained trail here for the boot path.

waypoints.name: Boulder field below the SE ridge
waypoints.note: First left off the PCT at a ~10-ft dead snag; boulder field lies to the north — follow cairns lined up with the snag to the field's high point.

waypoints.name: SE ridge avalanche slope
waypoints.note: Steep, brush-choked slope gains the southeast ridge; brush is very slick when wet or snow-covered and this line is avalanche-prone on all aspects — not recommended in unstable snow.

waypoints.name: Union Peak summit
waypoints.note: True summit, no maintained trail; open views down the Rainy Creek valley and along the PCT corridor toward Grizzly Peak.

waypoints.name: Reflection Lakes / Pinnacle Peak Trailhead
waypoints.note: ~35-car unpaved pullout on the south side of Stevens Canyon Road, directly across from Reflection Lakes; trail sign for Pinnacle Peak/Plummer Peak starts here.
waypoints.directions: Park at the Reflection Lakes pullouts on Stevens Canyon Road, about 1.4 miles east of the Paradise-Longmire Road junction and roughly 1.9 miles from the Paradise turnoff — an unpaved pullout on the south side of the road with room for about 35 cars, directly across from the largest of the Reflection Lakes. The signed trail for Pinnacle Peak/Plummer Peak starts right there; it's a maintained Mount Rainier National Park trail with no official number. Stevens Canyon Road is open roughly late May through late October, and this small lot commonly fills by mid-morning on summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Seasonal stream crossing
waypoints.note: A small seasonal stream crosses the switchbacks partway up; flows well early season but can run dry by late July-August.

waypoints.name: Cliff-band switchbacks below the saddle
waypoints.note: Trail steepens onto loose rock with exposed drop-offs on the final switchbacks before the saddle; NPS specifically warns of unstable rock and steep edges here, worse with lingering snow.

waypoints.name: Pinnacle Saddle
waypoints.note: T-intersection between Pinnacle and Plummer Peaks where the maintained trail ends; climber's boot path continues left/east to Pinnacle, right/west toward Plummer.

waypoints.name: Heather-and-talus boot path to Plummer's summit block
waypoints.note: Unmaintained Class 2 boot path across heather and loose talus with sparse cairns; easy to lose the path in cloud or on the descent.

waypoints.name: Plummer Peak summit
waypoints.note: Small rocky summit (7th-highest in the Tatoosh Range) with views north to Rainier and south to Adams, St. Helens, and Hood on clear days.

waypoints.name: North Fork Sauk Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 49 (6.4 mi off the Mountain Loop Hwy area); Northwest Forest Pass required and a self-issue Glacier Peak Wilderness permit at the kiosk; start of North Fork Sauk Trail #649.

waypoints.name: Pilot Ridge Trail junction
waypoints.note: Trail #649 forks with Pilot Ridge Trail #652 here; stay on #649 (the lower, riverside route) toward Mackinaw Shelter.
waypoints.directions: The first two miles are the gentlest of the trip: an easy grade through old-growth forest along the North Fork Sauk River, gaining only a few hundred feet.

waypoints.name: Red Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Red Creek on the climbers' path; hikers describe it as 'interesting but not difficult' at normal flow, tougher during peak snowmelt.
waypoints.directions: Two more nearly flat miles up the valley on good tread, crossing several small tributaries on the way. Red Creek is the first crossing that can actually stop you — it is manageable at normal flow but runs considerably higher during snowmelt or after heavy rain, and a pole or a sturdy stick helps with balance.

waypoints.name: Mackinaw Shelter
waypoints.note: Historic three-sided log shelter beside the North Fork Sauk River; the last easy, reliable camp before the trail turns steep and switchbacked toward White Pass.
waypoints.directions: A last easy mile beside the river brings you to the shelter clearing. Flat ground here is limited and a larger party will find it tight. Fill water before moving on, because the trail leaves the river from this point.

waypoints.name: White Pass (PCT junction)
waypoints.note: Trail #649 tops out on the Pacific Crest Trail after ~3.2 steep miles from Mackinaw Shelter; broad meadow/basin here with camping and a view down into Foam Basin.
waypoints.directions: The trail turns uphill in earnest and gains roughly 3,000 ft in sustained switchbacks through subalpine forest to a meadow junction with the Pacific Crest Trail, where Glacier Peak and the White Chuck side of the massif first come into view. Turn north on the PCT and follow it about a quarter mile to the pass. This is the last easy, reliable water before the high traverse.

waypoints.name: Glacier Gap crevasse crossing
waypoints.note: Crossing point between the White Chuck Glacier and White River Glacier near a tarn-dotted basin; crevasses open by late season here — rope up before continuing toward Kololo.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here. Traverse north below the White Mountain ridge into Foam Basin and White River Meadows, the usual base camp, either by way of Red Pass or by crossing snowfields to the notch west of Point 6770 and dropping into the White Chuck basin. From camp climb to Foam Pass and cross the White Chuck Glacier to the gap — this is glacier travel on largely featureless snow, so carry a track or the navigation skill to retrace it in cloud, and be roped for the crevasses low on the glacier, which can be fully open.

waypoints.name: Kololo Peaks (summit)
waypoints.note: Summit gained by a short rock scramble off the White River Glacier after the final low-angle ice/snow pitch; of the twin tops a short walk apart, the eastern one is the true high point by 10-15 ft, so tag both.
waypoints.directions: From the gap gain the flat shoulder at about 6,000 ft, then follow the connecting ridge north-northwest over a bulge near 7,200 ft, cross the small basin below the east summit, and continue west a quarter mile to a saddle at 7,400 ft. From the saddle, the ridge forming the east edge of the White River Glacier cirque leads to the final low-angle snow and a short talus-and-ledge scramble to the top. Expect a stretch of exposed blue ice a couple of hundred yards long on the White River Glacier — that section wants crampons and deliberate footwork rather than a plod.

waypoints.name: Necklace Valley Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR 68, 4.1 mi from US Hwy 2 at Skykomish; self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at the end of Forest Road 68, about 4.1 miles from US Highway 2 at Skykomish, at roughly 1,650 feet. A self-issue Alpine Lakes Wilderness permit and a Northwest Forest Pass are required at the trailhead kiosk.

waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River crossing
waypoints.note: Log or ford crossing of the East Fork Foss near an established camp; the first 5 miles gain only ~600 ft but this crossing can be tricky during high runoff.

waypoints.name: Jade Lake
waypoints.note: First of the Necklace Valley lakes and the common base camp for Hinman climbs; trail steepens sharply above the river crossing, gaining roughly 2,400 ft in about 3 miles to reach it.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Gap
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' path through boulder fields and heather gains this notch on the ridge crest above La Bohn Lakes; avoid the waterfall drainage to the left, routefinding is poor in fog.

waypoints.name: Hinman/Foss Glacier remnant snowfield
waypoints.note: Traverse of the shrinking glacier remnant below the west ridge; carry ice axe and crampons/microspikes for firm morning snow, and watch for isolated moats or crevasses late season.

waypoints.name: Mount Hinman summit
waypoints.note: Broad, multi-humped summit ridge where the true high point is ambiguous; final approach involves a short loose 4th-class scramble near the east end.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Glacier Creek Road (FR 39), 8 mi from Hwy 542; Northwest Forest Pass required for parking, self-issue Mt. Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at the end of Glacier Creek Road (Forest Road 39), about eight miles off Highway 542, at roughly 3,700 feet. A Northwest Forest Pass is required to park, and you self-issue a Mount Baker Wilderness permit at the kiosk there. Check current road status before you drive up, since conditions on FR-39 can vary.

waypoints.name: Kulshan Cabin site / creek crossings
waypoints.note: Established campsite at the old 1925 Kulshan Cabin site; bridged creeks along the lower trail provide reliable water before the climbers'-trail junction.

waypoints.name: Climbers' Trail / Hogsback Ridge junction
waypoints.note: Well-marked fork just past the Kulshan Cabin site: left continues to Heliotrope Ridge, right (climbers' path) climbs the Hogsback toward the Coleman Glacier.

waypoints.name: Hogsback Camp
waypoints.note: Camp sites scattered 6,000-6,200 ft along the moraine crest above the trees; standard bivy for Coleman Glacier and Colfax north-face routes.

waypoints.name: Coleman Glacier crevasse field
waypoints.note: Rope up crossing the glacier below Colfax; recent parties report a large crevasse forcing a lower, climber's-left detour.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund below the north face
waypoints.note: Cross the bergschrund at the base of Colfax's north face before the low-angle ice ramp; the schrund's character (snow bridge vs. open gap) varies season to season.

waypoints.name: Crux ice pillar (WI4)
waypoints.note: 30-40 ft near-vertical to slightly overhung water ice above the ramp; typically takes 5-6 screw placements.

waypoints.name: Colfax Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; descend toward the lower eastern summit, around its south side to the Colfax-Baker saddle, then down the Coleman-Deming route.

waypoints.name: Twin Lakes Trailhead
waypoints.note: Start of the High Pass Trail; Northwest Forest Pass required at the trailhead.
waypoints.directions: Drive Twin Lakes Road to its end at about 5,200 ft. The final miles are rough and deeply rutted, and many parties park short and walk them rather than risk the car. A Northwest Forest Pass is required; the signed High Pass Trail starts from the parking area.

waypoints.name: High Pass
waypoints.note: Leave the maintained trail here; drop and follow the climbers' path north and west toward the old Gargett Mine.
waypoints.directions: About a quarter mile up, the short spur to the Winchester Mountain lookout splits off — stay north on the High Pass Trail. It contours the west side of Winchester, dips through the minor saddle known as Low Pass with open views west to Tomyhoi, then climbs steadily to High Pass. This is maintained tread the whole way, roughly 750 ft of gain; Mount Baker comes into view south when you top out.

waypoints.name: Gargett Mine
waypoints.note: Old mine workings; last reliable water source until lingering snow patches high on the peak. Coordinate is the surveyed mine adit (elev 5708 ft) - parties camp in the basin just below at ~5400 ft.
waypoints.directions: Leave the maintained tread at the pass and follow the climbers' path north and west, dropping about 550 ft to the old mine workings. Tent space here is limited, so most parties bivy rather than camp properly. Fill up: the mine creek is the last easy water until lingering snow patches high on the peak.

waypoints.name: Notch (Mt. Larrabee NW rib)
waypoints.note: Reached after a long, unmarked sidehill traverse below Larrabee's southwest and west flanks; drop slightly beyond into the red talus/moraine bowl. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between Gargett Mine and the summit — estimated, not surveyed.
waypoints.directions: From the mine, traverse north across Larrabee's timbered southwest rib in the first quarter mile, then commit to a full mile of unmarked sidehill below Larrabee's west flank — steep talus, scree, heather and slick herbaceous slopes with no tread. A small scree chute at the end leads to the notch in Larrabee's rocky northwest rib. Do not start this traverse on wet grass or wet rock; helmets go on here and stay on, since rockfall is the defining hazard of the whole approach.

waypoints.name: South AmBo Saddle
waypoints.note: Scrambling and low 5th-class climbing begins here, below the rock feature climbers call 'De Gaulle's Nose'. Coordinate is a geometric interpolation (elevation-scaled) between Gargett Mine and the summit — estimated, not surveyed.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the notch, descend a steep dirt chute between snow and rock, then contour at roughly 5,800 ft above the moraine bowl. From there angle north through a series of steep gullies and ribs to the saddle. Route-finding, not difficulty, is what costs time on this section, and the red talus is loose throughout.

waypoints.name: American Border Peak summit
waypoints.note: Views to Mt. Larrabee, Canadian Border Peak, and the Pickets.
waypoints.directions: Follow a faint climbers' path along the crest for about two hundred yards, then traverse right onto slabby red ledges near a rock rib. A cleft just left of the rib and more slabby ledges gain a flat step on top of it; a down-sloping bench then crosses to the mouth of a steep snow gully, where a tall snow fin splits the gully and you take a moat on either side or the hole through the fin itself. From the notch above, two pitches of the Great Chimney lead to the top — a 5.3 entry, then a smooth 5.4 face move over a large chockstone and a squeeze so tight that packs have to be pushed through ahead of the climber. Above the chimney a dirty slabby trough, a row of horns and gaps, and one dramatically exposed step-across finish the climb.

waypoints.name: Slate Pass / Buckskin Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.note: On FR 5400-600 about 3.5 miles beyond Harts Pass; self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk, no fee required.
waypoints.directions: Drive the Harts Pass Road (FR 5400) up from Mazama and turn right at Harts Pass onto FR 5400-600 toward Slate Peak for about 3.5 miles to the Slate Pass trailhead at a switchback. It is one of the highest drivable roads in the state and typically does not clear of snow until early to mid summer, so check its status before committing.

waypoints.name: Whistler Cutoff – Middle Fork Pasayten Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Buckskin Ridge Trail drops via the Whistler Cutoff to meet the Middle Fork Pasayten River (Robinson Creek) Trail #478 in the valley bottom; steep, dusty descent losing ~1,900 ft.
waypoints.directions: Head north on Buckskin Ridge Trail #498 and take the cutoff that splits off about half a mile in. It drops steeply and dustily off the ridge, losing around 1,900 ft, to meet the Middle Fork Pasayten (Robinson Creek) Trail #478 on the valley floor.

waypoints.name: Fred's Pass
waypoints.note: Trail climbs from Berk Creek over this ridge-crest pass to drop into the upper Eureka Creek drainage — the standard link between the Middle Fork Pasayten valley and Eureka Creek basin on the shortest road approach to Lago/Dot.
waypoints.directions: Turn down-valley and follow the Middle Fork trail for roughly nine miles. The grade is easy but the going is slow — burn zones and hundreds of downed logs to step over or around — and the tread deteriorates the farther in you get. Near the head of the section the route turns up Berk Creek and climbs to the pass on the ridge crest.

waypoints.name: Lago–Carru Col
waypoints.note: Broad talus saddle between Mount Lago and Mount Carru at the head of Eureka Creek basin; can hold névé into midsummer and is the crux navigation point of the approach.
waypoints.directions: Drop off the pass into the upper Eureka Creek drainage and follow the basin through open meadows and larch groves. This is the last running water of the day, so fill here. Where the basin heads, leave the trail and climb off-trail up talus to the broad saddle between Carru and Lago.

waypoints.name: 7,400 ft Tarn Camp, Mount Lago north side
waypoints.note: Exposed alpine tarn camp used as high camp for the Lago/Dot traverse, reached by dropping off the col across Lago's rocky north slopes; intermittent snowmelt water only, no wood.
waypoints.directions: Contour east off the col across Mount Lago's north slopes, losing a couple of hundred feet to reach the tarn. The whole traverse is loose plate talus in the 6-12 inch range — worth wearing a helmet, since a party strung out across it will knock rock down onto itself.

waypoints.name: Point 8207
waypoints.note: Ridge high point passed on its north/climber's side above the tarn camp; easy dirt-and-rock walking with no route-finding issues above treeline.
waypoints.directions: Regain the crest above camp and follow it north. Taken direct, Point 8207 is the technical crux of the traverse: exposed Class 3-4 on rock that is surprisingly solid, with one short Class 4 step. Skirting it on the north side keeps the leg to easy dirt-and-rock walking. Either way there is no route-finding problem this high above treeline.

waypoints.name: Point 8165 Ledge Bypass
waypoints.note: An improbable, exposed 3rd-class ledge threads through cliffs on Point 8165's west side — the one technical move on an otherwise mellow ridge traverse toward Dot Mountain.
waypoints.directions: Continue north along the crest, which narrows and turns knife-edged in places with sustained Class 3 moves. Most parties skip Point 8165's true summit and cut onto its west side to pick up the ledge through the cliff band.

waypoints.name: Dot Mountain
waypoints.note: Talus-strewn summit at the north end of the Lago ridge system, gained via the final short traverse off Point 8165; broad, easy footing at the top.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the cliff band the ridge relents into a pleasant, mostly-dirt walk above treeline. The summit is an easy, non-technical walk-up along the crest — the difficulties of the traverse are all behind you.

waypoints.name: Ptarmigan-Dot Col
waypoints.directions: Only parties continuing to Ptarmigan Peak carry on past the summit. Follow the crest down off Dot over mild ground, losing about 400 ft to the saddle. There is no water anywhere on this ridge until a small tarn on Ptarmigan's south shoulder, roughly a mile further on.

waypoints.name: Esmeralda (Ingalls Way) Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of FR-9737 off North Fork Teanaway River Rd; small lot fills fast in summer, Northwest Forest Pass required, self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: From Cle Elum, head northeast on SR-970 about 5 miles, turn onto the Teanaway River Road and follow it roughly 23 miles to the road end. The small lot fills fast on summer weekends — a Northwest Forest Pass is required and there is a self-issue wilderness permit at the kiosk.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Pass
waypoints.note: Trail crests the pass with the first open view of Mount Stuart and the Ingalls Peaks; forks here, stay left/climber's-path toward Lake Ingalls rather than dropping right into Headlight Basin.
waypoints.directions: Take the Ingalls Way trail and stay left at the fork around 5,600 ft. Three miles of steady climbing brings you to Ingalls Pass, where Mount Stuart and the Ingalls Peaks come into view all at once. Fork again here: stay left on the climber's path toward Lake Ingalls rather than dropping right into Headlight Basin.

waypoints.name: Lake Ingalls
waypoints.note: Last reliable water before the summit scramble; camping and campfires are prohibited immediately around the lake to protect the fragile alpine basin, so treat/carry water here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse from the pass to Lake Ingalls, about a mile. This is the last reliable water before the summit, so fill and treat here — camping and campfires are prohibited around the lake to protect the basin.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Col (notch between South and North/main peaks)
waypoints.note: Scramble up slabs, talus and boulders from the lake to this notch below Dogtooth Spire; this is where the roped South Ridge route begins, distinct from the easier North Ridge to South Peak.
waypoints.directions: From the lake, scramble slabs, talus and boulders up to the notch between the North and South peaks, below Dogtooth Spire. Expect snow on this section in June and early July. This notch is where the roped South Ridge begins, and it is a different objective from the easier North Ridge scramble to the South Peak.

waypoints.name: Dogtooth Crags traverse
waypoints.note: Exposed traverse along the right side of the Dogtooth Crags on broken rock and slabs leading to the base bench; loose blocks and route-finding in fog are the main dangers here.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the right-hand side of the Dogtooth Crags on broken rock and slabs. Loose blocks are the main hazard, and this is the section people lose in fog — it is worth noting your line on the way in so you can reverse it.

waypoints.name: Bench below the red slab (start of roped pitches)
waypoints.note: Broad bench just below a distinctive large red slab; from the notch descend/traverse about 100 ft west to the base of a friction slab and rope up for the 3-pitch 5.4 ridge climb.
waypoints.directions: From the notch, descend and traverse roughly 100 ft west to the broad bench under the distinctive large red slab. Rope up here: the route is three pitches at 5.4, generally good rock with a few 5.2-5.3 moves and real exposure. The first pitch takes an obvious crack for close to a full rope length to a belay at a fixed piton on the slab.

waypoints.name: Ingalls Peak (North/main summit)
waypoints.note: True summit of Ingalls Peak; exposed but well-protected 5.4 climbing gains the top, descend by rappelling the route back to the col and reversing the approach.
waypoints.directions: Three pitches gain the true summit — exposed but well protected. Descend by rappelling the line you climbed, which goes in three raps on two 60 m ropes, or four on a single 60 m, using the same anchors, then reverse the scramble to the lake and the trail. Budget 3-4 hours for the approach and 3-5 hours for the climb; by August the whole basin gets hot and there is no shade above the lake.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Trailhead (Olympic NP)
waypoints.note: Olympic National Park entrance pass required for parking; wilderness permits (recreation.gov) needed for overnight camps on the Sol Duc/High Divide corridor.

waypoints.name: Sol Duc Falls
waypoints.note: Boardwalk viewpoint over the falls and junction with the Lover's Lane Trail; stay on the Deer Lake/High Divide Trail.

waypoints.name: Deer Lake
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp with bear wires; last easy water and flat tent sites before the steep climb to High Divide.

waypoints.name: Heart Lake
waypoints.note: Last reliable water before the dry, exposed Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie ridge section - top off here.

waypoints.name: High Divide - Cat Basin Trail Junction
waypoints.note: Maintained trail ends near here; the unmarked Bailey Range 'primitive route' splits off High Divide toward Cat Peak and off-trail routefinding begins.

waypoints.name: The Catwalk (Cat Peak-Mt. Carrie arete)
waypoints.note: Narrow, exposed ridge traverse on loose rock linking Cat Peak and Mount Carrie; a slip on the steep side-hill sections could mean a long uncontrolled fall.

waypoints.name: Ferry Basin
waypoints.note: Open meadow basin below Mount Ferry's south slopes with glacial tarns for camping/swimming, reached via a col just south of Stephen Peak (~5,900 ft).

waypoints.name: Mount Ferry
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 scramble off the main Bailey Range traverse near the Ferry-Pulitzer col; broad summit with views across Queets Basin to Mount Olympus.

waypoints.name: Olney Creek Road Gate
waypoints.note: Gated logging-road junction on Sultan Basin Road ~11.2-11.5 mi north of Sultan; no formal lot, park on the road shoulder.
waypoints.directions: From Sultan, follow Sultan Basin Road north about 11.2 to 11.5 miles to the gated junction with Olney Creek Road. Olney Creek Road is closed to public vehicle travel, so that gate is where the drive ends. There is no formal lot — park on the road shoulder at the junction. The day starts on foot from the gate, walking the closed logging road uphill.

waypoints.name: Second Switchback / Climbers' Path
waypoints.note: Closed Olney Creek logging road levels off at the second switchback here; a boot path breaks off to the right and follows the ridge crest toward the summit.

waypoints.name: Ridge Path Fade-Out
waypoints.note: The climbers' path peters out on the ridge crest around 4,000-4,200 ft; leave it and traverse cross-country southeast toward One Acre Lake.

waypoints.name: One Acre Lake
waypoints.note: Small alpine lake passed on its east side; last reliable water before the dry summit basin, but no confirmed shoreline coordinate found.

waypoints.name: Upper Drainage Tarns
waypoints.note: Ascend the drainage above the lake to a cluster of small tarns; flattish ground here works as a rough bivy for an overnight attempt.

waypoints.name: Summit Basin Gully
waypoints.note: Rocky basin/boulder field below the final ridge; the gully to the summit crest is wet, muddy, easy 4th class and can hold old snow or cornice debris into early summer — many parties carry a rope to rappel it.

waypoints.name: Mount Stickney Summit
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a short, airy walk/scoot across an exposed ridge section past a small plateau to the final rock hump.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Standard Eldorado Peak approach start; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road about 20 miles from Marblemount to the large Eldorado Creek trailhead parking area at road mile 20, around 2,100 ft. From the lot, backtrack a short distance downstream to find a log or ford crossing of the Cascade River and pick up the climbers' path heading east and upstream on the far bank. This is the shared Eldorado Peak approach, the same start the other Dorado Needle routes use.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp after the first two talus fields, en route to the higher glacier camps.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: High camp on the Inspiration Glacier shelf used for all Eldorado-area and Dorado Needle objectives.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north from Inspiration Glacier over this col onto the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier below the gendarmes
waypoints.note: Ascend the McAllister Glacier to just below Dorado Needle's line of gendarmes; this is the start of the NW Ridge, the easiest (1940 first-ascent) line at 5.4.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: Three pitches of class 5.4 rock past the gendarmes gain the true summit.

waypoints.name: Northwest Ridge approach point (NW of Dorado Needle)
Eldorado Creek Trailhead (Cascade River Road)
waypoints.note: Same start as the East Ridge; cross the Cascade River on a log downstream of the parking area.
waypoints.directions: Drive Cascade River Road to the Eldorado Creek trailhead at about road mile 20, elevation roughly 2,100 ft, and park in the trailhead lot. The climb starts by leaving the parking area and backtracking a short way downstream to find a log or a ford across the Cascade River, then picking up the climbers' path on the west side of Eldorado Creek. This is the same start the East Ridge uses; the trailhead-to-glacier approach is identical for both.

waypoints.name: Eldorado Creek Basin camp
waypoints.note: Open-basin camp option after the first two talus fields and a waterfall crossing.

waypoints.name: Eldorado/Inspiration Glacier high camp
waypoints.note: Base camp on the flat glacier shelf used to stage the Inspiration/McAllister glacier traverse.

waypoints.name: Inspiration–McAllister Glacier col
waypoints.note: Cross north across Inspiration Glacier to this col, then drop northwest onto the McAllister Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Descend the McAllister Glacier toward its southwest gap; navigate visible crevasses, especially late-season.

waypoints.name: Marble Creek–McAllister pass
waypoints.note: Lowest gap on the SW side of the glacier; cross to the small Marble Creek side glacier, generally on the pass's east side.

waypoints.name: Base of Southwest Buttress gully
waypoints.note: A snow-filled gully roughly 700 vertical feet below the pass leads to the start of the buttress climbing.

waypoints.name: Dorado Needle summit
waypoints.note: 9-pitch, Grade III, 5.7-5.8 buttress tops out on the true summit after a left-leaning corner on the upper ridge.

waypoints.name: Washington Pass Hairpin Turn
waypoints.note: Parking on the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 below Washington Pass.

waypoints.name: Spire Gully right - Alpenkuhl
waypoints.note: ~7 minute walk up from the hairpin to this sunny, south-facing crag on Spire Gully's right side.

waypoints.name: Graves Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Backcountry camping permit required (reserve online); trail begins on an old abandoned roadbed through old-growth fir and cedar.
waypoints.directions: Drive to the road end at Graves Creek in the park's southwest corner. Overnight trips need a reserved wilderness permit — Enchanted Valley is a quota zone and the summer-season permits are released online months ahead of the season — and a bear canister is required in the valley. The trail leaves the lot heading east up the East Fork Quinault River.

waypoints.name: Pony Bridge
waypoints.note: Crosses the East Fork Quinault River over a narrow gorge lined with maidenhair ferns; reliable water below the bridge.
waypoints.directions: The first two miles run nearly level on the old roadbed through big fir and cedar before a short, steep drop puts you down at river level. The bridge spans a narrow gorge; water is reachable below it, which matters because the trail then pulls away from easy river access for a while.

waypoints.name: O'Neil Creek Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp just past the O'Neil Creek crossing; good water source and a common first-night stop.
waypoints.directions: Four more miles of rolling old-growth rainforest — spruce, alder, bigleaf maple — with very little net gain. The camp sits immediately past the O'Neil Creek crossing, so if you are still walking uphill you have not reached it yet.

waypoints.name: Pyrites Creek Camp
waypoints.note: 12 designated sites split on both banks of Pyrites Creek; last reliable established camp before the valley.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-valley on the same gentle grade, crossing No Name Creek around mile 8 before reaching Pyrites. Sites are split across both banks of the creek, so check the far side before deciding the camp is full.

waypoints.name: Quinault River Bridge
waypoints.note: High footbridge 20 ft above the river that holds snow late into spring; use caution crossing when icy or snow-covered.
waypoints.directions: Above Pyrites the trail climbs gently for several more miles to a footbridge set roughly 20 ft above the water. It holds snow and ice later than the trail either side of it and the span feels exposed when covered — cross one at a time in those conditions.

waypoints.name: Enchanted Valley Chalet
waypoints.note: Historic 1930s chalet (closed to hikers due to riverbank erosion); leave the maintained trail here and head north/off-trail toward Chimney Peak's southwest ridge.
waypoints.directions: A short half mile past the bridge the rainforest opens onto the valley floor with Chimney Peak's cliffs and waterfalls filling the skyline. This is the end of easy travel — everything above is unmarked, with no cairns and no path. Some parties peel off the maintained trail short of the chalet rather than at it, so settle your own departure point before you drop the pack.

waypoints.name: Southwest Ridge Class 4 Step
waypoints.note: Short, exposed Class 4 step on loose rock near the top of the ridge; many parties place a short rappel here on descent.
waypoints.directions: Work north out of the valley and around onto the mountain's south and southwest flank, then follow a drainage up through steep timber and slide alder; this lower brush, not the rock, is the crux of the day for most parties. The ground opens onto heather and rock as you reach the ridge crest, where the Class 3 scrambling starts. Budget most of the summit day for this leg — it is roughly 4,700 ft of gain inside a mile, with route-finding through boulders and timber the whole way.

waypoints.name: Chimney Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the peak's namesake 100-ft rock chimney is visible on the west aspect, and the southeast face drops nearly 4,800 ft to Enchanted Valley in under a mile.
waypoints.directions: From the step it is only a short distance of Class 3 to the top. Keep well back from the southeast rim throughout — the drop to the valley floor is close to 4,800 ft in under a mile. The Olympics sock in fast and there is nothing marking the way back down, so fix your descent line while you can still see it rather than trusting the visibility to hold.

waypoints.name: PCT North Trailhead, Snoqualmie Pass (I-90 Exit 52)
waypoints.note: Large paved lot just north of I-90 exit 52; $5 self-issue Northwest Forest Pass fee, then north on the PCT into Alpine Lakes Wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Take I-90 to Exit 52 at Snoqualmie Pass. Cross under the freeway and take the first right; the PCT North (Commonwealth Basin) trailhead lot is a large paved lot on the right, at about 3,000 feet. Self-issue a Northwest Forest Pass ($5) at the trailhead before heading north on the Pacific Crest Trail into the Alpine Lakes Wilderness.

waypoints.name: Kendall Katwalk
waypoints.note: 150-yard path blasted into a steep granite cliff face on Kendall Peak's north ridge; narrow and exposed, can hold snow/ice into early July.

waypoints.name: Gravel Lake
waypoints.note: Reliable water at the lake outlet; established sites only, no fires permitted above 4,000 ft in this basin.

waypoints.name: Ridge Lake
waypoints.note: Established PCT campsites on the far shore and on the slope down to Gravel Lake; last easy camp before the Bumblebee Pass turnoff, 0.4 mi ahead.

waypoints.name: Bumblebee Pass
waypoints.note: Leave the PCT here on a steep, poorly-marked climber's path up a short gully; easy to walk past in fog or low light.

waypoints.name: Bumblebee Basin
waypoints.note: Small scenic basin on the far side of the pass, standard bivy for the climb; only intermittent tarns for water, check conditions before relying on them.

waypoints.name: Crux 5.6 Roofs (Pitch 2)
waypoints.note: Pull over the route's technical crux here on otherwise solid rock; rope up for pitches 1-4 before easing off into the Class 3-4 traverse.

waypoints.name: Mount Thomson
waypoints.note: True summit gained via a final scramble over ledges and cracks (P6); descend the East Ridge with one to three rappels from established stations.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin Trailhead (Cascade River Road pullout)
waypoints.note: Unmarked pullout at mile ~22 of Cascade River Road opposite Johannesburg Mountain, room for 6-8 cars; self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required.
waypoints.directions: The Boston Basin start is an unmarked climbers' pullout on Cascade River Road, about 21.7 miles from Marblemount at roughly 3,200-3,300 ft, sitting opposite Johannesburg Mountain. There is no trailhead sign of any kind, so watch your odometer rather than looking for signage — it is easy to drive straight past. The pullout holds six to eight cars and you need a Northwest Forest Pass to park. Camping in Boston Basin needs a North Cascades wilderness permit picked up in person at Marblemount, and the popular sites fill fast in the early-access lottery for peak summer weekends.

waypoints.name: Creek crossings through old-growth forest
waypoints.note: Climbers' path follows an old mining road then crosses several small streams in old-growth timber before switchbacking to treeline; reliable water but poorly marked in low light.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin low camp
waypoints.note: Designated moraine campsite with composting toilet at treeline; most parties continue higher for a shorter summit day.

waypoints.name: Boston Basin high camp
waypoints.note: Upper hardened camp on slabs/grass below Sharkfin Tower, closer to the Quien Sabe Glacier; the informal camps below Sharkfin are on this bench.

waypoints.name: Glacier rope-up point beneath Sharkfin Tower
waypoints.note: Where the boot path meets continuous snow on the Quien Sabe Glacier's lower-angle (north/left) side; rope up for crevasses here.

waypoints.name: Bergschrund crossing
waypoints.note: Narrow snow bridge crosses above and left of the bergschrund late-season; crevasses widen through August-September and the crossing point shifts year to year.

waypoints.name: Boston-Sahale Col
waypoints.note: Top of the glacier traverse beneath the Sharkfin face; gains the col between Sahale and Boston Peak before the final scramble.

waypoints.name: Sahale Mountain summit
waypoints.note: Short, exposed 3rd/4th-class scramble up the summit block from the col; the true summit block has fixed anchors used by many parties to rappel back to the col.

waypoints.name: Sunrise Mine Trailhead
waypoints.note: End of Forest Road 4065; follow Sunrise Mine Trail to Headlee Pass then around Sperry Peak to the Vesper/Sperry basin.

waypoints.name: Cairned pass toward Copper Lake / start of ledge traverse
North Face ledge-access notch (near True Grit; Fish & Whistle starts ~50 ft further west)
Vesper Peak north face
waypoints.note: Fish & Whistle starts from a large tree ~50 ft left of True Grit and climbs 5 pitches (5.10-) up the north face to near the summit.

waypoints.name: Slate Peak Trailhead (Buckskin Ridge TH)
waypoints.note: End of Slate Peak Road (FR-5400), a high-clearance gravel spur off Harts Pass Road; self-issue Pasayten Wilderness permit at the kiosk, road typically open only July-September.

waypoints.name: Slate Pass
waypoints.note: Saddle on Buckskin Ridge where the Buckskin Ridge/Middle Fork Pasayten trail junction is reached (~30 min from the TH) and the route leaves the ridge crest to drop steeply toward the Middle Fork Pasayten River.

waypoints.name: Fred's Lake
waypoints.note: Small subalpine lake with limited established sites reached via a climbing traverse off the Eureka Creek trail; standard first-night base camp for the Carru-Lago-Osceola cluster (~5 hrs in from the trailhead).

waypoints.name: Rolo Pass (ridge crest above Fred's Lake)
waypoints.note: Switchbacks out of the Fred's Lake basin gain this open ridge crest; views back northwest to Fred's Lake and east into the Eureka Creek headwater basin, the divide crossing point toward Shellrock Basin.

waypoints.name: Upper Eureka Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Rock-hop the Eureka Creek headwaters below Rolo Pass before climbing back up into Shellrock Basin; last reliable water before the summit day.

waypoints.name: Shellrock Basin
waypoints.note: Open meadow/talus basin near Shellrock Pass with tarn water, used as the high camp for Carru, Lago, and Blackcap summit pushes.

waypoints.name: Lago-Carru saddle
waypoints.note: Broad col between Mount Lago and Mount Carru; leave the basin here and gain Carru's southeast slope/ridge for the final scramble.

waypoints.name: Mount Carru
waypoints.note: True summit via class 2-3 talus and short rock on the southeast ridge; exposure enough on the final blocks to keep it interesting.

waypoints.name: Ross Dam Trailhead
waypoints.note: SR 20 milepost 134 parking lot; no parking pass is needed. Descend the Ross Dam Trail toward the lake to reach Ross Lake Resort and arrange a paid water-taxi pickup.
waypoints.directions: Drive SR 20 to the parking lot at milepost 134, roughly 28 miles east of Marblemount. No parking pass is needed to leave a car here.

waypoints.name: Big Beaver Landing (water-taxi drop)
waypoints.note: Ross Lake Resort's boat drops climbers here to skip miles of lakeshore trail; self-issue wilderness permit kiosk and start of the Big Beaver Creek Trail.
waypoints.directions: Walk down the Ross Dam Trail toward the lake and arrange a paid water-taxi pickup with Ross Lake Resort; the boat runs seasonally, costs about $35 one way, and drops climbers at Big Beaver Landing. Parties who cannot get a boat hike roughly 6 miles of lakeshore trail up the west side of Ross Lake instead.

waypoints.name: Luna Camp
waypoints.note: Established backcountry camp on the maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail through old-growth forest, roughly 8 trail miles above Big Beaver Landing.
waypoints.directions: Self-issue a wilderness permit at the kiosk, then follow the maintained Big Beaver Creek Trail up-valley through old-growth cedar. It is about 8 to 10 trail miles of easy walking, passing the Big Beaver backcountry camp, to reach Luna Camp.

waypoints.name: Access Creek crossing
waypoints.note: About 1.5 miles past Luna Camp, leave the maintained trail and ford Big Beaver Creek to pick up the faint, cairned Access Creek climbers' path.
waypoints.directions: Stay on the maintained trail about another 1.5 miles past Luna Camp, then leave it and ford Big Beaver Creek to pick up the faint, cairned climbers' path up Access Creek. This is the single easiest place on the trip to go wrong: in poor visibility parties have committed to the wrong drainage, so find the cairns marking the correct crossing before you commit.

waypoints.name: Access Creek headwaters basin
waypoints.note: Cairned climbers' path up the north flank crosses to the creek's south bank near 3,700 ft where brush thickens, then continues to good camping at the basin below the Luna-McMillan col.
waypoints.directions: Climb steep, pathless forest and heather along the north flank of Access Creek. The cairned path crosses to the south bank near 3,700 ft where the brush thickens, then continues to break out of the timber into the open, meadow-floored basin below Luna Peak, which is far less brushy than the drainages either side of it. Reports call it a few hours of reasonable but sustained hiking.

waypoints.name: Luna Col
waypoints.note: Notch between Luna Peak and a small tower on the Luna-McMillan arm; a small snowfield at the saddle usually provides running water and there's a good camp spot here or ~150 ft below on the east side.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-basin past the camping area at the headwaters, then climb a steep gully and heather system to the notch near 6,100 ft that first opens the view north into Luna Cirque. From there a long sidehill traverse of steep heather and talus works around Luna Peak toward Luna Pass, with one short genuinely steep section and cliff-band route-finding, before gaining the connecting ridge to the col. A small snowfield on the saddle usually gives running water.

waypoints.name: East Fury (ridge traverse start)
waypoints.note: Higher of Fury's twin summits and the start of the ~5.4 YDS, Grade III ridge traverse over three towers to West Fury; loose, exposed rock — rope up for the gendarmes.
waypoints.directions: Leave the col early on a light rack. Cross over Point 7360 and drop a red ledge system to a low-fifth-class crux tower, then climb the East Fury Glacier and arete to the summit. Most parties reach it around four to five hours out of camp.

waypoints.name: West Fury (Mount Fury, West Peak)
waypoints.note: True, officially-named summit of Mount Fury. Descend by reversing the ridge traverse to East Fury, then drop East Fury's east-side glacier/scree gully back to Luna Col.
waypoints.directions: Traverse the ridge over three loose towers, with short downclimbs and rappels connecting them. It is roughly 5.4 at its hardest, wildly exposed, and the rock is notoriously mobile choss rather than anything solid, so rope up for the gendarmes and expect two to three hours. Anchors are natural horns and slings you leave behind.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required; parking lot is just past the Downey Creek bridge on Suiattle River Road (FR 26), about 20 mi from Hwy 530.
waypoints.directions: Drive Suiattle River Road (FR 26) about 20 miles in from Highway 530; the parking area sits just past the Downey Creek bridge at roughly 1,450 feet. Display a Northwest Forest Pass. Check the road before you commit to the trip, because it is frequently washed out or gated well short of the trailhead, adding miles of walking or biking each way that none of the trail mileage here accounts for. The route is normally in condition July through September.

waypoints.name: Sixmile Camp
waypoints.note: Established camp along the easy, flat Downey Creek Trail #768 where the route leaves the maintained trail and turns east along Bachelor Creek.
waypoints.directions: Follow Downey Creek Trail #768 for 6.5 miles from the trailhead — easy, well-graded and mostly flat through forest, with a suspension-bridge crossing of Downey Creek.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford or log-cross Bachelor Creek to its south side here; the climbers' path above is badly overgrown with slide alder up to roughly 4,400 ft.
waypoints.directions: The maintained trail ends here; continue on the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path, staying on the north side of the creek at first, then ford to the south side at about the 9.5-mile mark. Treat it as a real creek crossing — harder and more dangerous in high water or early season.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake Pass
waypoints.note: Gap on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake (~5,880 ft), gained by switchbacks; begin the ~500 ft descent to the lake basin from here.
waypoints.directions: Climb the climbers' path above the crossing. Near 4,500 ft the tread largely disappears through a large avalanche-debris zone, so expect slow, brushy route-finding through slide alder and downed timber; above the debris the path climbs to the pass on the ridge crest northwest of Cub Lake.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake
waypoints.note: High camp with reliable water at the lake basin; Itswoot Ridge, reached by traversing further, is the alternate camp some parties use instead.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft off the pass into the lake basin. These are snow slopes into midsummer and this is normally the crux navigation of the approach day when they are covered.

waypoints.name: Dome Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the Dome Glacier's crevasses toward the Dome-Sinister col; a bergschrund spans the glacier and requires finding a solid snowbridge.
waypoints.directions: Most parties push on from the lake basin up onto Itswoot Ridge for high camp, then traverse climbers' paths and snow benches through the upper basins, staying near 7,000 ft, to gain the glacier. Rope up for glacier travel and carry crevasse-rescue gear before starting across.

waypoints.name: Dome-Sinister col
waypoints.note: Saddle between Dome and Sinister Peaks; from here contour on an easy snowfield around to Sinister's south side to reach the loose southwest gully.
waypoints.directions: Cross over the Dome–Chikamin col and descend the crevassed Chikamin Glacier to about 7,200 ft, then traverse right (east) across the glacier to the col. The bergschrund guarding it can be hard to cross in late season and has sometimes required a short rappel to get down onto or across it.

waypoints.name: Sinister Peak
waypoints.note: True summit, just under a mile east of Dome Peak along the connecting ridge; reached via the loose southwest gully to the upper west ridge.
waypoints.directions: From the col contour around on an easy snowfield to Sinister's south side, then climb the loose, unpleasant gully to gain the upper west ridge and scramble Class 2–3 along the ridge to the top. Loose rock in the gully is the main hazard — move fast and keep the party out of each other's fall line; some parties skip it and take the exposed Class 3+ ridge directly from the col.

waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River / Necklace Valley Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk; trail follows an old railroad grade along the East Fork Foss River.

waypoints.name: East Fork Foss River crossing
waypoints.note: Log/boulder-hop ford of the East Fork Foss River with no bridge; can be a difficult, cold crossing at high water or early season.
waypoints.directions: The first five miles are the flattest of the route — barely 600 ft of gain along the river through old-growth forest, past established camps, with a spur path near mile 4 dropping to the water. Save your legs here, because everything above the crossing is steep.

waypoints.name: Jade Lake
waypoints.note: First and largest of the Necklace Valley 'gem' lakes, reached after a steep 2,400 ft climb in 3 miles above the river crossing; established campsites and reliable water, but campfires are banned above 4,000 ft in the wilderness.
waypoints.directions: Immediately past the river the trail turns steep and stays that way, gaining roughly 2,400 ft in three miles over large boulders and tree roots on rugged, minimally maintained tread. This is the crux of the approach for footing and stamina, and it is slow in both directions.

waypoints.name: Scree scramble to La Bohn Lakes
waypoints.note: Steep scree/boulder gully gains roughly 950 ft in half a mile above the valley floor to La Bohn Lakes; the boot path is faint and easy to lose, especially in fog or on lingering snow patches.
waypoints.directions: Continue up-valley past Emerald Lake, where a seasonal stream at the north end is the reliable water, toward Opal and Cloudy Lakes at the head of the valley — the maintained trail effectively ends here and boot paths fan out. From the Opal Lake camp area, pick up the crude unmaintained path climbing beside La Bohn Creek, the outlet stream of the La Bohn Lakes. It is west-facing and unshaded, hot in the afternoon, and there is no dependable water once you leave the valley floor.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Gap
waypoints.note: Broad saddle often called the geographic center of the Alpine Lakes Wilderness; routes toward Mt. Hinman, Iron Cap Mountain, and La Bohn Peak's east ridge all branch from here.
waypoints.directions: The path eases at the lowest La Bohn Lake; follow the shore and heather benches north to the upper lake, then make a short talus-and-heather traverse east to the broad saddle. Confirm you are at the right saddle before committing to any slope east of it — USGS maps label the gap roughly two-thirds of a mile southeast of its true position, and the ground east of the wrong gap ends in cliffs above Lake Rowena. Lingering snow can mask the correct line into early summer.

waypoints.name: La Bohn Peak
waypoints.note: Class 2-3 tag-on of roughly 700-1,000 ft from the gap up the east ridge; broad rocky summit with views of Mt. Hinman, Mt. Daniel, and the Necklace Valley lakes below.

waypoints.name: Dingford Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Standard access point via FR-56/Middle Fork Snoqualmie River Road; no day-use fee is currently charged at this specific trailhead (per USFS), though a free self-issue wilderness permit is required beyond it for Alpine Lakes Wilderness travel, and the road washout beyond this point means biking or hiking the closed roadbed toward Dutch Miller Gap.
waypoints.directions: FR-56 up the Middle Fork Snoqualmie to the lot is heavily potholed and rutted; parties in low-clearance cars routinely park short and walk the last stretch, which adds to an already long day.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Lake
waypoints.note: Standard high camp for the route, roughly 10 mi in via the Middle Fork Snoqualmie trail/old roadbed then a steep, unmaintained forested slog above a river ford near the old Dutch Miller Gap Trail; seldom-visited alpine lake below the Overcoat Glacier basin.
waypoints.directions: The continuation of the road past the gate is roughly 7-8 miles of old roadbed to Hardscrabble Horse Camp, and most parties bike it rather than walk it. Beyond that the Dutch Miller Gap Trail runs east along the north bank; the tread is reasonable but summer thimbleberry buries the rocks underfoot. Leave the trail about a mile before it swings toward Williams Lake and ford the river: it can run thigh-to-waist deep, and it is colder and higher on the way back than it was in the morning.

waypoints.name: Rock benches above Overcoat Glacier
waypoints.note: Higher alternate camp on open benches used to shorten summit day; this bivy option sits at roughly 6,600 ft.
waypoints.directions: Above the ford the ground climbs steeply through brush into a rocky corridor of waterfalls and steep faces before opening onto snow and benches. Snow lingers here well past midsummer. The awkward part is a sloping rock step partway up, which is markedly harder to downclimb than to climb and is worth noting for the return.

waypoints.name: Notch on Overcoat Peak's north ridge (Overcoat Col)
waypoints.note: Contour east from camp to this notch to gain the upper Overcoat Glacier; a col of the same name and elevation (~6,800 ft) sits beneath Chimney Rock's east face.
waypoints.directions: Only a couple of hundred feet of net gain, but it is a rising traverse over benches and old snow rather than a walk. The glacier starts immediately on the far side, so rope up and fit crampons at the notch rather than after stepping onto it.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Glacier crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the glacier's lower snowfields toward the snow finger below the east face; expect deep crevasses and weak, undermined snow bridges on this rapidly retreating glacier.
waypoints.directions: Drop onto the upper glacier from the notch and work toward the snow finger below the east face. Most parties time this route for the tail end of summer, when the crevasses are open and visible and the rock above is clear of snow; earlier in the season the bridges are the thing that will catch you out.

waypoints.name: Snow finger to east face
waypoints.note: Find the snow finger leading off the glacier onto the east face here, then pick up the Class 3-4 ledges and steep gully toward the summit block.
waypoints.directions: The finger rises off the top of the glacier and is steep enough that crampons and a second tool are the norm. A crevasse commonly cuts it partway up and has to be turned. Near the dark towers at its top, move off snow onto rock and round the corner east to reach the ledge system.

waypoints.name: Overcoat Peak
waypoints.note: True summit; the final ~400 vertical ft is Class 4/low-5.0 ledges and a steep gully on the east side, with a small summit register.
waypoints.directions: The gully has solid holds but a few tall steps force committing, exposed moves, and most parties pitch it out on small cams and nuts in mediocre rock rather than soloing it. Sort the descent before you commit: the damp dihedral below is normally rappelled twice, not downclimbed.

waypoints.name: Downey Creek Trailhead
waypoints.note: Self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk; trail starts just past the Downey Creek bridge, 20.6 mi up Suiattle River Road (FR 26) from SR 530.
waypoints.directions: Drive Suiattle River Road (FR 26) 20.6 miles from SR 530; the trailhead is just past the Downey Creek bridge. Self-issue a wilderness permit at the kiosk and display a Northwest Forest Pass.

waypoints.name: Sixmile Camp / Bachelor Creek Trail junction
waypoints.note: Maintained Downey Creek Trail 768 ends here at an established camp; the unmarked, unmaintained Bachelor Creek Trail climbs steeply south toward Bachelor Meadows.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Downey Creek Trail (768/792) roughly 6.5 miles of gentle, well-graded walking through old-growth forest. Recent Forest Service work has added boardwalks and new log bridges, so this is the easy day; the maintained trail simply ends at the established camp.

waypoints.name: Bachelor Creek log crossing
waypoints.note: Cross Bachelor Creek on a downed log below Bachelor Meadows — last reliable water before the high camps; dense alder and old blowdown make this stretch the route-finding crux of the approach.
waypoints.directions: From the north side of the crossing, pick up the unmaintained Bachelor Creek climbers' path. It starts as a clear boot-track climbing steeply beside the creek before easing into switchbacks, then gets overgrown with salmonberry and vine maple through the meadows around 4,000 ft. Dense alder and old blowdown make this the route-finding crux of the whole approach; the path is easy to lose and the creek can run swift in early season.

waypoints.name: Cub Lake pass
waypoints.note: Forested saddle overlooking Cub Lake; descend steep talus and switchbacks about 500 ft to the lake's east shore before regaining the ridge toward Itswoot.
waypoints.directions: Keep climbing on switchbacks, crossing an avalanche chute that holds snow late and is exposed to slide activity into early summer, then duck back into trees on climber's left. Around 5,900 ft the path tops out on the forested ridge overlooking the lake.

waypoints.name: Itswoot Ridge camp
waypoints.note: Open bivy sites on the ridge crest with a stream running down from Spire Point; continuous snow above roughly 6,800 ft typically requires crampons.
waypoints.directions: Drop about 500 ft on steep talus and switchbacks to the lake, which also has good camping, skirt its north shore, and regain the ridge heading toward Itswoot. A stream draining the Spire Point basin gives reliable water at the ridge camp.

waypoints.name: Spire Col
waypoints.note: Standard high camp on Itswoot Ridge with the first view north across the Ptarmigan Traverse; the climb starts about a quarter mile east along the ridge, not on the slabby ledges directly above camp.
waypoints.directions: Hike north up Itswoot Ridge, staying on talus on its west side near the stream to bypass the rock towers directly above camp; the crest itself is only walkable in short gentle stretches. Snow is usually continuous above about 6,800 ft, so crampons and an axe come out here. You can either climb the moderate 30-degree snow straight to the col or skirt the left edge of the snowfield on rock.

waypoints.name: Class 4 summit chimney
waypoints.note: Short, loose class 4 chimney through scree gains the summit ridge crest — the technical crux, exposed and prone to kicked-down rock from parties above.
waypoints.directions: From the col, gain roughly 400 to 500 ft on talus and broken ledges to the base of the face, about a quarter mile along the ridge. Loose talus leads to the foot of the chimney, which is only about 30 ft of climbing on solid granite with good holds but is where parties rope up.

waypoints.name: Spire Point
waypoints.note: Tiny summit block holds one climber at a time; descend via two 60m rappels back down the chimney/ledge system to Spire Col.
waypoints.directions: Above the chimney, traverse exposed class 3 ledges across the face to the ridge crest and around onto the west side, with well over a thousand feet of air below. The last 50 ft goes as a 5.6 friction slab or, alternatively, cracks just left of the slab with better holds. Belay it: the horn holds one climber at a time, so parties take turns.

waypoints.name: Washington Pass Hairpin Turn
waypoints.note: Parking on the Hairpin Turn pullout on SR-20 below Washington Pass.

waypoints.name: Stuart Lake Trailhead
waypoints.note: Northwest Forest Pass required for parking; self-issue overnight wilderness permit at the kiosk if camping June 15-Oct 15.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Lake
waypoints.note: Take the left fork staying high on the ridge/shoreline north, avoiding the many spurs that drop to the water.

waypoints.name: Outlet dam creek crossing
waypoints.note: Cross the outlet creek at or just below the small dam on the lake's north end, then pick up the climbers' path on the far side, south for about 100 yards.

waypoints.name: 3rd/4th class rock step
waypoints.note: Short step of rock above a talus clearing; pull up on tree roots and branches with the rock face on your left rather than climbing it head-on.

waypoints.name: Boulder camp in the flats
waypoints.note: Low-impact camping on rock and gravel among boulders just below the col; no reliable water at this camp.

waypoints.name: Colchuck Balanced Rock Col
waypoints.note: Well-cairned path through open forest/hillside (~1 hr from the dam) gains the col; reaching the true summit block from here requires additional 4th/5th-class scrambling.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Trailhead
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits at roughly 3,400 to 3,700 ft on Glacier Creek Road 39. The road washed out in December 2025 and reopened to vehicles in August 2026 after repairs; it has washed out before, so check its status before committing.

waypoints.name: Heliotrope Ridge Camp
waypoints.directions: Trail 677 climbs through old-growth forest and flower-filled avalanche chutes, with a couple of unbridged creek crossings that are awkward early season or after rain. At about 2.25 miles the maintained trail forks; the left branch goes to the Coleman Glacier overlook, so take the right climbers' path that drops toward the moraine. Past the former Kulshan Cabin site near 4,800 to 5,000 ft, the last reliable running water, the path climbs steeply up the crest of the Hogsback lateral moraine to the usual camps between about 6,500 and 7,200 ft, roughly 3 to 3.5 miles and 3,000 ft above the car. Above camp there is no water except what you melt.

waypoints.name: Coleman Headwall Base
waypoints.directions: Rope up for glacier travel and cross the broken lower Coleman, generally trending up toward 8,000 ft to meet the North Ridge tracks before dropping back down and cutting under the Roman Nose to reach the base near 8,500 ft. This crossing is a real route-finding crux that changes year to year, with big crevasses to weave around, questionable snow bridges, and sometimes a committing, barely-reversible jump or a short vertical step to get established. Leave camp in the dark (starts between 11 p.m. and 4:30 a.m. are typical) so you are past the exposed crossing and the lower face before the sun brings rock and ice down off the headwall and the Black Buttes.

waypoints.name: Mount Baker Summit
waypoints.directions: Roughly a dozen pitches of sustained 45 to 50 degree neve and ice lead up the face: hard, dirty ice on leftward-trending traverses low down with rockfall exposure from a choss band above, then short steeper steps and an 800 ft band of brittle, plated 60 to 80 degree ice that takes screws well despite looking suspect. A bergschrund near 10,000 ft is the other crux and its lip often forces a short, occasionally overhanging step, sometimes belayed or lowered across off a screw or picket. Above it the angle relents to moderate snow and then an easy slope onto the summit plateau; 8 to 12 hours camp-to-summit is typical.

waypoints.name: Barlow Pass Trailhead
waypoints.note: Paved-road parking lot at end of Mountain Loop Highway; Northwest Forest Pass required, walk past the gate onto Monte Cristo Road.

waypoints.name: Weden Creek Trail #724 split
waypoints.note: Leave the gated Monte Cristo Road here (just before the Sauk River crossing) and pick up the signed, steep single-track into Gothic Basin.

waypoints.name: Weden Creek crossing
waypoints.note: Ford Weden Creek on the climbers' path roughly a mile up the trail; can run high with snowmelt in early season.

waypoints.name: Rocky water gully, mile 3.25
waypoints.note: First of several creek/gully crossings where the trail turns noticeably rockier and steeper for the final push into the basin.

waypoints.name: Gothic Basin tarns
waypoints.note: Two small tarns just below Foggy Lake mark the basin; camping is extremely limited and fragile, day-hike this section if possible.

waypoints.name: Weden Pass
waypoints.note: Traverse south through steep talus and heather for a bit over a mile from the basin to gain this pass on the ridge crest between Gothic Basin and Sheep Gap's peaks.

waypoints.name: Summit notch rappel
waypoints.note: From Weden Pass traverse SW toward the notch, dropping to ~4900 ft on a brushy dirt ramp to skirt cliff bands, then regain the notch; a short Class 4 step here requires downclimbing or a short (~50-60 ft) rappel.

waypoints.name: Sheep Gap Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit register shows only a handful of visits per decade; expect a long day (10-17 hrs) and possible snow/ice axe conditions even in late season.
